questions.hintContent: Notice how fast the reaction began and which body system the throat symptoms involve.
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem includes airway symptoms, apply the ABCs and choose the option that protects the airway.
questions.stem: A nurse puts on latex gloves to start an IV for a 29-year-old client. Within 5 minutes, raised wheals appear on the client's forearm, the client says, “My throat feels tight,” and the client's voice is hoarse. The nurse has already removed the gloves. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply cool compresses to the wheals to relieve the itching and swelling
Document a latex allergy in the health record and on the allergy band
Stay with the client, assess the airway, and call the rapid response team
Give a prescribed oral antihistamine and recheck the skin in 30 minutes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cool compresses ease itching but do nothing for an airway that may be closing.
Incorrect. The allergy must be documented, but only after the airway emergency is managed.
Correct. Wheals within minutes plus throat tightness and hoarseness signal an immediate allergic reaction involving the airway, a possible anaphylaxis emergency that needs help now.
Incorrect. An antihistamine may be part of treatment, but an oral dose acts slowly, does not protect a closing airway, and waiting 30 minutes delays emergency help.
questions.rationale: Hives or wheals that appear within minutes of latex contact are an immediate allergy, not the delayed allergic contact dermatitis that appears 1 to 3 days later. Throat tightness and hoarseness mean the airway is involved, so this can progress to anaphylaxis. The nurse stays with the client, assesses airway and breathing, and gets emergency help right away. Documenting the latex allergy is the tempting answer because it is a real safety step, but it never comes before a threatened airway.
questions.takeaway: Hives plus throat tightness or hoarseness after an allergen is an airway emergency: get help before comfort or documentation.

rows: Started benzoyl peroxide gel 5 days ago; face is dry, pink, and peeling.
Eczema behind the knees; one scratched patch is now warm, swollen, more painful, and draining yellow fluid. Temperature 38.4 °C (101.1 °F).

questions.stem: The dermatology clinic nurse reviews the telephone messages in the exhibit. Which client should the nurse call back first?
options: The 6-year-old with eczema
The 15-year-old using benzoyl peroxide
The 42-year-old with psoriasis
The 31-year-old with poison ivy
optionRationales: Correct. A scratched patch that is warm, swollen, more painful, and draining, with fever, suggests a secondary infection that needs prompt treatment.
Incorrect. Dryness, pinkness, and peeling in the first week of benzoyl peroxide are expected effects.
Incorrect. A stable client asking about a moisturizer has a routine teaching need.
Incorrect. New spots a few days into poison ivy are common from oil left on skin or items or slower-reacting areas; the client is stable.
questions.rationale: Scratching breaks the weak eczema barrier, and broken skin can become infected. Warmth, swelling, increasing pain, drainage, and fever are signs of a secondary infection, which is an unexpected and potentially spreading problem. New poison ivy spots are the most tempting distractor, but they are expected in the first days and come from leftover oil, not from spread through blister fluid. Expected effects and routine questions can wait until the client with signs of infection has been called.
questions.takeaway: Expected findings can wait; signs of infection in scratched skin (warmth, swelling, drainage, fever) get the first call.

questions.hintContent: Recall how each age group differs in its skin response to irritants and allergens.
questions.hintStrategy: Watch for absolute words such as "always" and "within minutes"; they often signal a wrong answer.
questions.stem: An 83-year-old resident began using a new scented body lotion 6 days ago. Today the nurse notes faint pink, mildly itchy skin only where the lotion was applied. The resident's daughter says, “It can't be the lotion. She would have reacted right away.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Older adults have drier skin, so mild pink itching like this is most likely just dryness.”
“Allergic reactions to skin products appear within minutes, so something else is the cause.”
“Older adults have thinner skin that absorbs more, so their reactions are usually stronger.”
“Older adults react more slowly and less intensely, so a reaction can appear late and look mild.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Older adults do have drier skin, but the redness is limited to where the lotion was applied, which points to the lotion rather than dryness.
Incorrect. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed reaction that usually appears 1 to 3 days or more after exposure.
Incorrect. Aging skin is thinner, but older adults have slower, weaker immune skin responses, so reactions are usually milder, not stronger. Infants have the strongest irritant response.
Correct. Older adults have slower, less intense skin reactions, so a reaction to a product can appear days later and look mild, and it is easy to miss.
questions.rationale: Age changes how the skin reacts: infants have the strongest irritant response, adults have most allergic contact dermatitis, and older adults have slower, less intense reactions. A faint rash limited to the lotion site that appears days after starting the product fits a muted, delayed reaction in an older adult. The tempting answer is that allergic reactions happen right away, but only immediate hives behave that way; contact dermatitis is delayed. The nurse should report the finding and stop the product per the plan of care rather than dismiss it as dry skin.
questions.takeaway: Older adults react to irritants and allergens more slowly and less intensely, so a mild, late rash can still be a product reaction.

questions.hintContent: Think about where eczema shows up at different ages and what conditions run in the same families.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true or false for this disorder at this age; a correct finding for another disorder is still false here.
questions.stem: A 6-month-old is brought to the clinic because the infant rubs his face on the crib sheets and seems itchy. Both parents have asthma. Which findings support atopic dermatitis (eczema) in this infant? Select all that apply.
options: Dry, rough, red patches on both cheeks
Red, shiny skin limited to the area the diaper covers
Linear streaks of vesicles on one forearm
A family history of asthma and allergies
Dry, itchy patches on the outer surfaces of the arms and legs
Thick, well-defined plaques with silvery scale on the knees
optionRationales: Correct. In infants, eczema often appears on the cheeks.
Incorrect. Red, shiny skin where the diaper touches is irritant diaper dermatitis from urine and stool.
Incorrect. Linear streaks of vesicles suggest poison ivy, an allergic contact dermatitis.
Correct. Eczema commonly runs in families with asthma and allergies.
Correct. The outer arms and legs are typical eczema sites in infants; skin creases become typical in older children.
Incorrect. Thick, well-defined plaques with silvery scale describe psoriasis.
questions.rationale: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing, very itchy condition caused by a weak skin barrier, and it often begins in infancy in families with asthma and allergies. Location changes with age: infants have patches on the cheeks and outer arms and legs, while older children have them in the antecubital and popliteal creases. Psoriasis plaques, diaper-area irritation, and linear vesicles each point to a different disorder. Matching the pattern and location to the age group is the key skill.
questions.takeaway: Infant eczema = itchy dry patches on the cheeks and outer limbs, often with a family history of asthma or allergies.

questions.hintContent: Recall why the timing of the moisturizer matters for skin that loses water easily.
questions.hintStrategy: In "needs further teaching" items, look for the one statement that is false; the correct statements are the distractors.
questions.stem: The nurse taught the parent of a 9-year-old with eczema in the antecubital and popliteal areas how to care for the child's skin at bath time. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I'll keep his bath short and use lukewarm water instead of hot water.”
“I'll wait an hour after his bath, when his skin is fully dry, to put on cream.”
“I'll use a mild, fragrance-free cleanser and skip the bubble bath.”
“I'll gently pat his skin with a soft towel instead of rubbing it dry.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A short, lukewarm bath is correct; hot water dries the skin.
Correct. This statement needs correction: moisturizer should go on within a few minutes, while the skin is still slightly damp, to lock in water.
Incorrect. Mild, fragrance-free cleansers are correct; harsh soaps and bubble baths irritate the weak barrier.
Incorrect. Patting dry is correct and avoids friction on irritated skin.
questions.rationale: Eczema skin has a weak barrier that loses water quickly. The routine is a short lukewarm bath with a mild cleanser, a gentle pat dry, and a thick fragrance-free moisturizer applied right away while the skin is still damp. Waiting until the skin is fully dry lets the water evaporate first, which defeats the purpose. The other statements are all correct steps, which is why a quick reader may miss that timing is the error.
questions.takeaway: Eczema bath routine: short, lukewarm, mild cleanser, pat dry, and moisturize within minutes while still damp.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Separate measures that reduce itch or scratch damage from measures that add eczema triggers.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, test each option on its own: does it help the barrier and avoid known triggers?
questions.stem: A 5-year-old with atopic dermatitis wakes several times each night scratching, and the parent has noticed small scabs on the child's arms. Which measures should the nurse recommend to break the itch–scratch cycle? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a thick, fragrance-free moisturizer right after the evening bath
Have the child wear soft cotton gloves at night
Dress the child in soft cotton pajamas instead of wool
Add a heavy wool blanket so the child stays very warm
Keep the child's fingernails trimmed short
Apply a scented lotion at bedtime to soothe the itching
optionRationales: Correct. Moisturizing right after bathing repairs the barrier and reduces itch.
Correct. Cotton gloves at night reduce damage from scratching during sleep.
Correct. Soft cotton is less irritating than wool or scratchy fabrics.
Incorrect. Wool irritates the skin, and heat and sweating are eczema triggers.
Correct. Short nails cause less skin damage when the child scratches.
Incorrect. Fragrance is a common eczema trigger.
questions.rationale: In eczema, itch leads to scratching, scratching damages the barrier, and the damaged barrier itches more. Breaking the cycle means reducing itch (moisturize, avoid triggers such as fragrance, heat, and sweating) and reducing the damage scratching causes (short nails, cotton gloves at night, soft cotton fabrics). A warm wool blanket sounds comforting but adds two triggers at once. Broken skin from scratching can also become infected, so preventing it matters.
questions.takeaway: Break the itch–scratch cycle: moisturize, avoid fragrance, heat, and wool, keep nails short, and use cotton gloves at night.

questions.hintContent: Match the shape, scale, and location to each disorder, and remember that redness may not look red on dark skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the key feature of each option (location, shape, history) and match it to one disorder.
questions.stem: A 46-year-old client with dark brown skin comes to the clinic for a rash that has been present for several months. Which assessment finding is most consistent with psoriasis in this client?
options: Clusters of small vesicles on the wrist that match the shape of a bracelet
Well-defined violet to dark brown plaques with gray scale on the elbows and knees
Dry, itchy, dark patches in the elbow creases that have come and gone since childhood
A single larger oval patch on the trunk, then smaller oval patches a week later
optionRationales: Incorrect. Vesicles shaped like an object suggest allergic contact dermatitis.
Correct. Psoriasis forms thick, well-defined plaques on the elbows and knees; in darker skin they may look violet or dark brown with gray scale.
Incorrect. Itchy patches in skin creases since childhood suggest eczema, which can also look darker in dark skin.
Incorrect. A herald patch followed by smaller oval patches suggests pityriasis rosea.
questions.rationale: Psoriasis speeds up skin-cell turnover so cells pile up into thick, well-defined plaques, usually on the elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back. Textbook pictures show red plaques with silvery scale, but in darker skin the plaques may look violet or dark brown with gray scale. The eczema option is tempting because eczema also looks darker in dark skin, but it appears as dry, itchy patches in the skin creases and typically starts in childhood. Knowing how conditions look across skin tones prevents missed diagnoses.
questions.takeaway: Psoriasis in darker skin may look violet or dark brown with gray scale, on the elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back.

questions.hintContent: Think about the emotional effect of a visible, chronic skin condition.
questions.hintStrategy: In therapeutic communication items, choose the response that reflects feelings and is open-ended; eliminate advice, facts that skip feelings, and false reassurance.
questions.stem: A 27-year-old client with plaque psoriasis on the arms and legs tells the nurse, “I stopped going to the pool with my friends. People stare at my skin like it's contagious.” Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: “Many people with psoriasis feel self-conscious. A support group could really help you.”
“Psoriasis is not contagious, so you can simply explain that to people who stare.”
“It's normal to feel that way. A light swim shirt might help you feel more comfortable.”
“That sounds painful. How has your skin been affecting the way you feel about yourself?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A support group may help later, but generalizing and referring right away moves past what this client is feeling now.
Incorrect. The fact is true, but it skips the client's feelings and puts the burden of explaining on the client.
Incorrect. Validating is supportive, but jumping to a solution before exploring the feeling closes the conversation too early.
Correct. It acknowledges the feeling and uses an open-ended question to explore the effect on self-image.
questions.rationale: Psoriasis plaques are visible and can hurt self-esteem, so the nurse should ask how the client feels about their skin. A therapeutic response acknowledges the emotion and invites the client to say more. The most tempting wrong answer is the accurate statement that psoriasis is not contagious; teaching can come later, but leading with facts dismisses the feeling the client just shared. Suggesting a support group or a swim shirt is supportive, but offering solutions before exploring the feeling closes the conversation too early.
questions.takeaway: When a client shares feelings about a visible skin condition, acknowledge and explore the feeling before teaching facts.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Recall what wakes up an overactive immune response in the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it stresses or injures the body; remove options that describe normal self-care.
questions.stem: A 38-year-old client whose psoriasis had been in remission for a year now has new plaques. Which factors in the client's recent history may have triggered the flare? Select all that apply.
options: A scraped knee where a new plaque has formed
Drinking more water during hot weather
Strep throat infection treated 3 weeks ago
Switching to a fragrance-free moisturizer
Starting a stressful new job last month
Hugging a cousin who also has psoriasis
optionRationales: Correct. Skin injury can trigger new plaques at the injured site.
Incorrect. Fluid intake is not a psoriasis trigger.
Correct. Infections can trigger psoriasis flares.
Incorrect. Moisturizing is part of psoriasis care and does not trigger flares.
Correct. Stress is a common flare trigger.
Incorrect. Psoriasis is an immune-related disorder and is not contagious.
questions.rationale: Psoriasis is chronic and immune-related, so treatment aims for remission rather than cure. Flares can be triggered by stress, skin injury, infections, and some medications, and a new plaque at the site of a scrape is a classic example of injury triggering disease. Psoriasis does not spread by contact, which is why hugging a relative with the condition is not a cause. Identifying triggers helps the client prevent the next flare.
questions.takeaway: Psoriasis flares are triggered by stress, skin injury, infection, and some medications, never by contact with another person.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Compare the mechanism behind psoriasis, eczema, and acne.
questions.hintStrategy: Each option describes a real mechanism; match each one to its disorder and keep the one that fits the stem.
questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with psoriasis asks the nurse, “Why does my skin pile up into these thick, scaly patches?” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Your immune system speeds up skin cell growth, so cells pile up in days instead of a month.”
“Your skin barrier is weak, so it loses moisture and lets irritants in, which causes scale.”
“Extra oil and dead skin cells plug your hair follicles, and bacteria build up underneath.”
“A fungus is growing in the top layer of your skin and causing it to thicken and flake.”
optionRationales: Correct. In psoriasis the immune system shortens skin-cell turnover from about a month to a few days, so cells build up into plaques.
Incorrect. A weak barrier that loses moisture describes atopic dermatitis (eczema).
Incorrect. Oil and dead cells plugging follicles describes acne.
Incorrect. Psoriasis is immune-related, not a fungal infection.
questions.rationale: Normally new skin cells take about a month to reach the surface and shed. In psoriasis, an immune-related process speeds this to a few days, so cells pile up into thick, well-defined plaques with scale. The weak-barrier explanation is tempting because eczema is also chronic and itchy, but that mechanism describes eczema, not psoriasis. Understanding the mechanism helps the client accept that treatment controls the disease rather than cures it.
questions.takeaway: Psoriasis = immune-driven, too-fast skin-cell turnover (days instead of a month) that piles up into scaly plaques.

questions.hintContent: Recall how benzoyl peroxide is applied, what side effects are expected, and how long it takes to work.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each instruction independently; eliminate options that increase irritation or stop treatment too early.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old with mild acne on the face, chest, and upper back is starting over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide gel. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a thin layer to the whole affected area, not just to individual pimples
Stop the gel if the acne has not cleared after 1 week
Use white towels and pillowcases because the gel can bleach fabric
Scrub the skin firmly with a washcloth before each application
Use a non-comedogenic moisturizer if the skin becomes dry
Expect some dryness, redness, or peeling during the first weeks
optionRationales: Correct. A thin layer over the whole area treats forming lesions as well as visible ones.
Incorrect. Improvement takes several weeks, so stopping after 1 week is too soon.
Correct. Benzoyl peroxide bleaches towels, pillowcases, clothing, and hair.
Incorrect. Scrubbing increases irritation and inflammation; wash gently twice a day.
Correct. A moisturizer that will not clog pores eases dryness without worsening acne.
Correct. Mild dryness, redness, and peeling are expected when starting the gel.
questions.rationale: Benzoyl peroxide is the first-line OTC acne treatment; it kills bacteria and unplugs oil ducts. Clients should wash gently, apply a thin layer to the whole affected area, expect some dryness at first, use a non-comedogenic moisturizer, protect fabrics, and keep using it for several weeks. Scrubbing is the tempting wrong choice because teens often believe acne comes from dirt, but scrubbing worsens inflammation. Stopping early is the most common reason treatment "fails."
questions.takeaway: Benzoyl peroxide: wash gently, thin layer to the whole area, expect dryness, protect fabrics, and give it several weeks.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Link each product to the part of acne formation it targets.
questions.hintStrategy: Watch for options that swap two correct facts; verify each half of the statement.
questions.stem: A 19-year-old with blackheads and whiteheads asks the nurse how salicylic acid differs from the benzoyl peroxide a friend uses. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Salicylic acid kills bacteria in the follicle, while benzoyl peroxide only dries out the oil glands.”
“Salicylic acid exfoliates dead skin cells; benzoyl peroxide mainly shrinks the oil glands.”
“Salicylic acid exfoliates and calms inflammation; benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs ducts.”
“Both kill acne bacteria in the follicle, but only salicylic acid also removes dead skin.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The actions are reversed; benzoyl peroxide is the one that kills bacteria.
Incorrect. The salicylic acid half is right, but benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs oil ducts rather than shrinking the glands.
Correct. Salicylic acid removes dead skin cells and reduces inflammation; benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs oil ducts.
Incorrect. Salicylic acid does remove dead skin, but it does not kill bacteria; benzoyl peroxide is the product that kills acne bacteria.
questions.rationale: Acne forms when sebum and dead skin cells plug a follicle and bacteria grow inside it. Benzoyl peroxide, the first-line OTC product, kills the bacteria and unplugs the oil ducts. Salicylic acid exfoliates, removing the dead cells that help form the plug, and reduces inflammation. The reversed option is tempting because both products target the plugged follicle, so the student must know which one acts on bacteria.
questions.takeaway: Benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs ducts; salicylic acid exfoliates and reduces inflammation.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Recall the chain of events from puberty hormones to an inflamed pimple.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the statement that explains the mechanism; eliminate common myths about dirt, contagion, and food.
questions.stem: The school nurse explains to a 13-year-old how acne forms. Which statement by the student shows correct understanding?
options: “I get pimples because I don't wash enough, so I need to scrub my face several times a day.”
“Germs on my skin cause pimples, so I'll need an antibiotic to make them go away.”
“Hormones make my skin oilier, so cutting greasy foods from my diet will clear it.”
“Hormones make my skin oilier, and oil and dead skin clog my pores so germs can grow there.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Acne is not caused by dirt, and scrubbing worsens inflammation.
Incorrect. Skin bacteria do play a role, but they grow only after oil and dead cells plug the follicle, and many cases are treated without antibiotics.
Incorrect. The hormone part is right, but oil on the skin comes from the glands, not greasy foods, so diet changes alone will not clear acne.
Correct. Puberty hormones increase sebum, and sebum plus dead cells plug the follicle where skin bacteria grow and cause inflammation.
questions.rationale: At puberty, hormones make the oil glands produce more sebum. Sebum and dead skin cells plug the hair follicle, forming a comedone, and bacteria that normally live on the skin grow inside and cause red papules and pustules. The belief that acne comes from poor washing is the most tempting misconception and leads teens to scrub, which increases irritation and scarring. Correct understanding supports gentle care and adherence to treatment.
questions.takeaway: Acne = hormones → more sebum → sebum plus dead cells plug the follicle → bacteria and inflammation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Think about what is on the skin right now and how to get rid of it.
questions.hintStrategy: For "first" questions, choose the option that removes the cause before options that treat symptoms.
questions.stem: A 44-year-old landscaper calls the occupational health nurse 20 minutes after pulling poison ivy vines off a fence with bare hands. No rash has appeared yet. Which action should the nurse instruct the client to take first?
options: Apply over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream to both hands now
Watch the skin for 2 to 3 days and call back if a rash appears
Wash the hands and forearms with soap and cool water right away
Wash the clothing and gloves that touched the vines in hot water
optionRationales: Incorrect. Hydrocortisone treats inflammation after a rash appears; it does not remove the oil.
Incorrect. Waiting leaves the oil on the skin, where it can cause a rash and spread to other items.
Correct. Washing with soap and cool water as soon as possible removes the plant oil before it causes a reaction.
Incorrect. Washing clothing and gear is an important step to prevent re-exposure, but removing the oil from the skin comes first.
questions.rationale: Poison ivy contains an oil that causes allergic contact dermatitis, with a rash that usually appears 1 to 3 days after contact. The first priority after exposure is to remove the oil by washing the skin with soap and cool water as soon as possible, and then to wash clothing, gloves, and tools. Applying a steroid cream is tempting because it is a familiar treatment, but it treats symptoms that have not started and leaves the cause on the skin. Removing the trigger always comes before treating the reaction.
questions.takeaway: After poison ivy contact, wash the skin with soap and cool water right away, then wash clothes, gloves, and tools.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Identify where the plant oil could still be present.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask of each option, "Did this touch the plant or the oil?" Only those items carry the risk.
questions.stem: Two days after a family camping trip, the father develops streaks of itchy vesicles on both legs, and the provider confirms poison ivy. The family dog ran through the same brush. Which items could cause new rashes in family members if they are not washed? Select all that apply.
options: The fluid from the father's blisters
The jacket he wore while hiking through the brush
The dog's fur
A cup the father drank from after washing his hands
The garden gloves and tent stakes he used while clearing brush
The father's hiking boots and socks
optionRationales: Incorrect. Blister fluid does not contain the oil and does not spread the rash.
Correct. Clothing that brushed the plant carries the oil.
Correct. Pets can carry the oil on their fur and spread it to people.
Incorrect. After washing his hands, the cup is not a source of plant oil.
Correct. Oil remains on gloves and tools until they are washed.
Correct. Plant oil stays on shoes and clothing and can cause rashes later.
questions.rationale: Poison ivy dermatitis is caused by plant oil, not by anything in the rash itself. The oil can stay on skin, clothing, shoes, gloves, tools, and pet fur, and it causes new rashes when someone touches those items. Blister fluid is the most tempting wrong answer because the blisters look contagious, but the fluid does not spread the rash. Teaching the family to wash every item that touched the plant prevents new cases.
questions.takeaway: Poison ivy spreads by the plant oil on skin, clothes, tools, and pet fur, not by blister fluid.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall which test detects a delayed contact allergy and how long it takes.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each described procedure to its name and purpose, then pick the one that fits the suspected diagnosis.
questions.stem: A 36-year-old hairstylist with a recurring hand rash is scheduled for patch testing to find the cause. After the nurse explains the test, which statement by the client indicates understanding?
options: “A sample of my blood will be tested for antibodies to the hair products I use.”
“Small amounts of possible allergens are taped to my skin and checked over a few days.”
“The provider will scrape off some skin scales and look at them under a microscope.”
“A small piece of the rash will be removed and examined to see if it is cancer.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Patch testing is done on the skin, not with a blood sample.
Correct. A patch test places small amounts of possible allergens on the skin and checks the sites over the next few days for a delayed reaction.
Incorrect. Scraping scales for microscopy is used to look for fungus.
Incorrect. Removing tissue to check for cancer describes a biopsy.
questions.rationale: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed immune reaction, so the patch test is designed to detect delayed responses: possible allergens are taped to the skin and the sites are checked over several days. A hairstylist is exposed to dyes, perfumes, and chemicals that are common allergens. The skin scraping option is tempting because it is also a skin test, but it looks for fungus rather than allergy. Knowing what each test detects helps clients prepare and return for the readings.
questions.takeaway: Patch test = possible allergens taped to the skin and read over several days to confirm allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Consider who the cream was prescribed for and how strong steroids affect thin skin.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client is using a medication not prescribed for them, the best answer stops it and involves the prescriber.
questions.stem: The parent of a 3-year-old with an eczema flare says, “My sister gave me the strong steroid cream her dermatologist prescribed for her. I've been putting it on his face and body twice a day this week.” Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Tell the parent to stop the sister's cream and ask the child's provider for a prescribed treatment
Tell the parent to keep using the cream but only once a day to lower the total steroid dose
Tell the parent to stop it on his face but keep using it on his body until the flare clears
Tell the parent to stop the cream and use a thick fragrance-free moisturizer after each bath
optionRationales: Correct. Clients should use only steroids prescribed for them, in the strength and for the time ordered, and the child needs a provider-directed plan.
Incorrect. Reducing the frequency still exposes the child's face and thin skin to a strong steroid that was not prescribed for him.
Incorrect. Stopping it on the face is reasonable because facial skin absorbs more, but the body would still get a strong steroid that was never prescribed for the child.
Incorrect. Stopping the cream and moisturizing are both right, but the child's active flare still needs a provider-directed treatment plan.
questions.rationale: Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation, but long-term or high-potency use thins the skin and can cause visible vessels, easy bruising, stretch marks, and lighter patches. Young children and facial skin are especially vulnerable because they absorb more. The safe rule is to use only steroids prescribed for that client, for the time ordered, and never someone else's medicine. Lowering the dose is tempting because it sounds like harm reduction, but it still continues an unsafe, unprescribed drug.
questions.takeaway: Never use someone else's steroid cream; use only the prescribed product, strength, and duration.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Recall the goals of contact dermatitis care and the adverse effects of topical steroids.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, pick the finding that matches the goal of the treatment; eliminate new problems and adverse effects.
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with allergic contact dermatitis from a nickel belt buckle has avoided the buckle and used a prescribed topical corticosteroid and cool compresses for 5 days. Which finding best indicates that treatment is effective?
options: The redness is lighter, but two new vesicles formed near the waistband
The skin under the cream looks thinner and shinier than before
The client reports less itching, and no new vesicles have formed
The rash looks unchanged, but the compresses ease the itching briefly
optionRationales: Incorrect. Lighter redness is a good sign, but new vesicles mean the reaction is still active or the trigger has not been fully removed.
Incorrect. Thin, shiny skin is an adverse effect of topical steroids.
Correct. Less itching and no new lesions are the expected outcomes of removing the allergen and reducing inflammation.
Incorrect. Brief relief from compresses is helpful, but an unchanged rash after 5 days does not show that the treatment is working.
questions.rationale: Care for contact dermatitis is to identify and remove the trigger, soothe the skin, use prescribed medicines, and evaluate the response. Effective treatment shows less itching and redness, no new lesions, and no signs of infection from scratching. Thinner, shinier skin may look "smoother," which is why it can be mistaken for improvement, but it is a sign of steroid skin thinning. New vesicles or a rash that looks unchanged after several days mean the plan needs to change.
questions.takeaway: Dermatitis is improving when itching and redness decrease, no new lesions form, and there are no signs of infection.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Identify the likely allergen and think about how to protect the client during this admission.
questions.hintStrategy: When a safety risk is known, choose the action that removes the hazard now over actions that delay or mask it.
questions.stem: During an admission interview, a 58-year-old client says, “The last time I was in the hospital, I got an itchy, blistered rash on my hands where the nurses touched me with their rubber gloves.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document a latex allergy in the record and use latex-free gloves
Ask the provider to order a patch test before any gloves are used
Use latex-free gloves now and tell the next nurse during handoff report
Tell the client to report any itching the next time gloves are used
optionRationales: Correct. The history suggests a latex allergy, so it must be documented to alert all staff, and latex-free (for example, nitrile) gloves should be used.
Incorrect. Care cannot wait for testing; the safe step is to avoid latex now.
Incorrect. Latex-free gloves are right, but a verbal handoff reaches only one nurse; documenting the allergy alerts every caregiver and department.
Incorrect. Watching for symptoms is reasonable, but it waits for a reaction instead of preventing exposure to a suspected allergen.
questions.rationale: A rash where gloved hands touched the skin, appearing after exposure, suggests a latex allergy. The nurse documents the allergy so every caregiver avoids latex and switches to latex-free gloves and supplies. A patch test may later confirm the allergen, which makes it tempting, but safety now comes from avoiding the suspected trigger. Repeated exposure in a sensitized person can cause worse reactions, including immediate hives and airway involvement.
questions.takeaway: Suspected latex allergy: document it and switch to latex-free supplies immediately; do not wait for testing.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the reported effects are expected and how long benzoyl peroxide takes to work.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client wants to stop a treatment, check whether the complaint is an expected effect; if so, reassure and support adherence.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old who started benzoyl peroxide gel 4 days ago tells the nurse, “My face is a little dry and pink, and my pimples aren't any better. I'm going to quit using it.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “That pinkness means your skin is irritated, so stop it for a few days and then restart it.”
“Put on a thicker layer twice as often for the next few days so it can start working faster.”
“Stop using it every day, and just put a dab on each new pimple whenever one shows up.”
“Some dryness is expected, and acne takes several weeks to improve. A light moisturizer can help.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pausing can help severe irritation, but mild dryness and pinkness are expected early effects, and stopping delays the weeks of steady use acne needs.
Incorrect. Thicker, more frequent applications increase irritation without speeding results.
Incorrect. The gel should cover the whole affected area regularly, not single spots.
Correct. Mild dryness and redness are expected early, improvement takes weeks, and a non-comedogenic moisturizer eases dryness.
questions.rationale: Benzoyl peroxide commonly causes dryness, redness, or peeling when started, and acne takes several weeks to improve. Teens often stop early because they expect fast results, so the nurse reassures, explains the time frame, and suggests a non-comedogenic moisturizer. Using more product is tempting for a frustrated teen, but thick or frequent layers only increase irritation. Spot treatment misses lesions that are forming under the skin.
questions.takeaway: Early dryness with benzoyl peroxide is expected; keep using a thin layer for several weeks and add a non-comedogenic moisturizer.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Notice the shape and location of the rash and what touches the skin there.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the assessment question that targets the strongest cue in the stem.
questions.stem: A 30-year-old client comes to urgent care with an itchy, red rash made of small papules in a round patch just below the navel. The rash started 2 days ago. Which question should the nurse ask first to help identify the cause?
options: “Has anyone you live or work with had a similar itchy rash lately?”
“Do you wear jeans or a belt with a metal snap that touches that spot?”
“Have you had a fever, chills, sore throat, or body aches this past week?”
“Did you have eczema, asthma, or hay fever when you were a young child?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Asking about contacts would point toward an infectious rash, which the localized, object-shaped pattern does not suggest.
Correct. A round, itchy rash in one spot below the navel suggests allergic contact dermatitis from a metal snap or buckle, such as nickel.
Incorrect. Systemic symptoms are not the key clue for a localized, item-shaped rash.
Incorrect. Atopic history relates to eczema, which appears in skin creases rather than in one round patch.
questions.rationale: The first step in contact dermatitis care is to identify the trigger. A rash shaped like an object and located where that object touches the skin, such as a jeans snap or belt buckle below the navel, strongly suggests allergic contact dermatitis to metal. Asking about household contacts is tempting because it is a common rash question, but it fits infectious rashes, not a single patch shaped like an item. The answer to the snap question directs the plan: avoid the item and confirm with a patch test if needed.
questions.takeaway: A rash in the exact spot an object touches (snap, buckle, watch, ring) points to allergic contact dermatitis; ask about that object first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Compare the prescribed duration with actual use and recall what long-term topical steroids do to the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: When findings match a known adverse effect, choose the option that reports it and corrects the medication use.
questions.stem: A 61-year-old client has applied a high-potency corticosteroid cream to psoriasis plaques on both forearms twice daily for 5 months, although it was prescribed for 2 weeks. The surrounding skin is now thin and shiny with visible small blood vessels and several bruises. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Reassure the client that shiny skin means the psoriasis plaques are clearing
Report the findings to the provider and review how long the cream was prescribed
Teach the client to apply the cream only to plaques, never to the skin around them
Document the skin changes and recheck the forearms at the next visit
optionRationales: Incorrect. Shiny, thin skin is steroid-induced thinning, not improvement.
Correct. Thin, shiny skin with visible vessels and bruising are adverse effects of long-term topical steroid use, so the provider must reassess the plan.
Incorrect. Applying steroid only to plaques is correct teaching, but it does not address 5 months of overuse or the adverse effects the provider must reassess.
Incorrect. Documentation is needed, but waiting until the next visit lets the steroid damage continue; the provider needs to know now.
questions.rationale: Long-term topical corticosteroid use thins the skin, producing thin, shiny skin, visible small blood vessels, easy bruising, stretch marks, and lighter patches. This client used a high-potency product far longer than prescribed. The nurse reports the adverse effects and reinforces using the steroid only as prescribed and for the time ordered. Reassurance is the tempting wrong answer because the skin may look smoother, but that appearance is damage, not healing.
questions.takeaway: Thin, shiny skin with visible vessels and bruising after months of topical steroids is an adverse effect to report.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Listen to what the teen's statement may mean beyond the skin condition.
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem includes a possible threat to safety, address safety before physical or teaching needs.
questions.stem: A 16-year-old with severe acne on the face and back has stopped going to school. During the visit, the teen says quietly, “Everyone would be better off if I just disappeared.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Explain that benzoyl peroxide usually improves acne within weeks
Encourage the teen to join a club or team to rebuild confidence
Refer the teen to a school counselor to talk about feeling left out
Ask the teen directly whether they are having thoughts of suicide
optionRationales: Incorrect. Teaching about acne treatment ignores a possible safety risk.
Incorrect. Encouraging activities skips assessment of the statement the teen just made.
Incorrect. Counseling support is helpful, but referring first hands off a possible safety risk without assessing whether the teen is suicidal.
Correct. The statement may signal suicidal thinking, and asking directly is the first step in assessing the teen's safety.
questions.rationale: Visible skin conditions can seriously affect a teen's self-esteem, leading to embarrassment and withdrawal from friends and school. A statement such as "everyone would be better off if I disappeared" is a possible warning sign of suicidal thinking, and safety comes before the skin condition. Asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea; it opens the door to help. Teaching about acne treatment is tempting because the visit is about acne, but it ignores the most urgent problem.
questions.takeaway: A teen's hopeless statement outranks the skin problem: ask directly about suicidal thoughts first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Recall which everyday actions can trigger a psoriasis flare.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the teaching that removes the harmful behavior rather than one that only modifies it.
questions.stem: A 41-year-old client with psoriasis says, “Every night I scrub the scales off my elbows with a loofah and a stiff brush so they look smoother.” Which teaching by the nurse is most important?
options: “Scrubbing can injure the skin and trigger new plaques, so moisturize instead.”
“Scrub only once a week so that the scale has time to build back up.”
“Use a fragrance-free soap so your skin is less irritated while you scrub.”
“Try to keep your stress low, since stress is a common trigger for new plaques.”
optionRationales: Correct. Skin injury can trigger psoriasis flares, and moisturizing softens the skin without damaging it.
Incorrect. Scrubbing less often still injures the skin each time.
Incorrect. Fragrance-free products are gentler, but the scrubbing itself is the injury that can trigger new plaques.
Incorrect. Stress is a true flare trigger, but this teaching does not address the scrubbing injury the client just described.
questions.rationale: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-related disorder, and skin injury is one of the known flare triggers, along with stress, infections, and some medications. Scrubbing plaques with a stiff brush injures the skin and can cause new plaques to form. Teaching focuses on moisturizing, avoiding scratching or injuring the skin, managing stress, and keeping follow-up appointments. Reducing how often the client scrubs is tempting as a compromise, but any scrubbing is still injury.
questions.takeaway: In psoriasis, avoid injuring the skin (scrubbing, scratching) because injury triggers new plaques; moisturize instead.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Separate routine, predictable care from tasks that require clinical judgment.
questions.hintStrategy: For delegation SATA, eliminate any option with the words assess, teach, or evaluate.
questions.stem: An RN is caring for a hospitalized 8-year-old with an atopic dermatitis flare and is planning tasks for an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). Which tasks can the RN delegate to the UAP? Select all that apply.
options: Evaluate whether the topical steroid is reducing the redness
Give the child a short, lukewarm bath with a fragrance-free cleanser
Apply the plain, fragrance-free moisturizer right after the bath
Teach the parent how to recognize the triggers that cause flares
Change the child's bed linens to soft cotton sheets
Assess the scratched areas for signs of infection
optionRationales: Incorrect. Evaluating the response to a medication requires RN judgment.
Correct. Bathing with specified water temperature and cleanser is routine hygiene care within the UAP role.
Correct. Applying a plain, non-medicated moisturizer is routine skin care that can be delegated.
Incorrect. Teaching is an RN responsibility.
Correct. Changing linens is a routine task within the UAP role.
Incorrect. Assessment requires the RN's clinical judgment.
questions.rationale: The RN can delegate routine, predictable care for a stable client, such as bathing, applying a plain moisturizer, and changing linens, while giving clear instructions (lukewarm water, fragrance-free products, soft cotton). Assessment, teaching, and evaluation stay with the RN. Assessing for infection is the tempting wrong choice because the UAP sees the skin during the bath; the UAP should report what they see, but the RN performs the assessment. Clear instructions protect the fragile eczema barrier.
questions.takeaway: Delegate routine skin care (bath, plain moisturizer, linens); keep assessment, teaching, and evaluation with the RN.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Compare the timing, pattern, and number of people affected in each type of contact dermatitis.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding into one of two columns (irritant or allergic) before choosing.
questions.stem: Several housekeepers at a hotel developed hand rashes after the staff switched to a new cleaning solution. The occupational health nurse assesses one housekeeper. Which findings suggest irritant contact dermatitis rather than allergic contact dermatitis? Select all that apply.
options: Her hands are red, dry, cracked, and burning
Coworkers using the same solution have similar dry, cracked hands
Itchy vesicles end in a sharp line where her gloves stop
She had a similar rash 2 days after using the product at a previous job
Redness and burning began during her very first shift using the solution
A patch test was positive for an ingredient in the solution
optionRationales: Correct. Red, dry, cracked, burning skin is the typical look of irritant dermatitis.
Correct. An irritant damages anyone's skin with enough exposure, so many workers are affected.
Incorrect. Vesicles shaped like an item suggest an allergic reaction to that item.
Incorrect. A rash appearing days after re-exposure following an earlier exposure suggests sensitization, which is allergic.
Correct. Irritant dermatitis can occur on the first exposure because it is direct chemical damage, not an immune response.
Incorrect. A positive patch test confirms an allergy.
questions.rationale: Irritant contact dermatitis is direct damage to the skin barrier from chemicals, soaps, or detergents. It needs no prior sensitization, can occur on the first exposure, affects anyone with enough exposure, and causes red, dry, cracked, burning skin. Allergic contact dermatitis requires sensitization, appears 1 to 3 days after re-exposure, is shaped like the allergen, and is confirmed with a patch test. The glove-line vesicles are tempting because the housekeeper works with chemicals, but that pattern points to an allergic reaction to the gloves.
questions.takeaway: Irritant = first exposure, many people affected, dry cracked burning skin; allergic = prior sensitization, delayed, shaped like the item, positive patch test.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.hintContent: Recall the categories of risk factors for skin disorders: genes, illness, medications, nutrition, and exposures.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each finding against the list of risk categories; a well-controlled disease is still a risk factor.

rows: Type 2 diabetes; HIV infection, well controlled
Prednisone 10 mg orally daily for the past 6 months

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the health history of a client at a wellness visit. Refer to the exhibit. Which findings increase this client's risk for skin disorders? Select all that apply.
options: Balanced diet with a BMI of 23
Type 2 diabetes
Long-term prednisone use
HIV infection
Indoor occupation
Family history of psoriasis
optionRationales: Incorrect. Good nutrition supports healthy skin; poor nutrition is the risk factor.
Correct. Diabetes is a chronic illness that weakens skin defenses and slows healing.
Correct. Steroids may thin the skin and increase sun sensitivity.
Correct. HIV/AIDS is a chronic illness that increases the risk of skin disorders.
Incorrect. Working indoors does not increase skin disorder risk and reduces sun exposure.
Correct. Psoriasis runs in families, so genetics raise the client's risk.
questions.rationale: Risk factors for skin disorders include genetics and family history, age and sex, chronic illness (diabetes, HIV/AIDS, obesity, poor circulation), medications (steroids, antibiotics, chemotherapy, antifungals), poor nutrition, and exposure to irritants and allergens. This client has four: two chronic illnesses, long-term prednisone, and a family history of psoriasis. "Well controlled" may make HIV seem like a non-factor, but it remains a chronic illness that raises risk. A healthy diet and indoor work are protective, not risks.
questions.takeaway: Skin risk rises with family history, chronic illness (diabetes, HIV), steroids and other risky drugs, and poor nutrition.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Consider what thin newborn skin means for body temperature and what vernix does.
questions.hintStrategy: For "first" actions with a newborn, think thermoregulation; eliminate options that remove protective coatings or add heat loss.
questions.stem: A full-term newborn has just been born and placed skin-to-skin on the parent's chest. The newborn's skin is wet, and a white, cheesy coating fills the skin folds of the groin and underarms. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Scrub the cheesy coating out of the skin folds with a soft washcloth
Place a knit cap on the newborn's head to prevent heat loss from the scalp
Gently dry the newborn and cover the newborn and parent with a warm, dry blanket
Take the newborn's axillary temperature to check for early heat loss
optionRationales: Incorrect. The coating is vernix, which protects and moisturizes the skin and is absorbed on its own; scrubbing damages the skin.
Incorrect. A cap helps prevent heat loss, but the wet body loses heat by evaporation, so drying and covering come first.
Correct. Newborn skin is thin, so the newborn loses heat quickly; drying and covering prevents heat loss.
Incorrect. Temperature checks are needed, but a wet newborn is already losing heat, so the nurse acts to prevent heat loss before measuring it.
questions.rationale: Newborn skin is thin, which has two effects: the newborn loses heat quickly and absorbs substances easily. The first priority for a wet newborn is preventing heat loss by drying and covering. The white, cheesy coating is vernix caseosa, which protects the skin and is absorbed on its own, so it should not be scrubbed or bathed off. Removing the vernix is tempting because it looks like something to clean, but it serves a protective purpose.
questions.takeaway: Wet newborn: dry and cover first to prevent heat loss, and leave the protective vernix in place.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Recall which newborn findings are expected and need no treatment.
questions.hintStrategy: When a finding is normal for age, the best answer reassures and prevents harm; eliminate answers that treat a normal finding.
questions.stem: The parent of a 3-day-old points to tiny white bumps on the newborn's nose and chin and asks whether they should be squeezed. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “These are whiteheads, so wash them twice a day with an acne cleanser to clear them.”
“These look like erythema toxicum, a harmless newborn rash that fades within a week.”
“These are milia from blocked oil glands. I'll ask the provider about a cream for them.”
“These are milia from blocked oil glands. Don't squeeze them; they fade in a few weeks.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Acne cleansers are not used on newborn skin, which absorbs products easily.
Incorrect. Erythema toxicum is also harmless, but it is red blotches with yellow-white centers, not tiny white bumps on the nose and chin.
Incorrect. The identification is right, but milia need no treatment, and newborn skin absorbs creams easily.
Correct. Milia are tiny white bumps from blocked oil glands; they are harmless, should not be squeezed, and go away on their own.
questions.rationale: Milia are tiny white bumps on a newborn's nose, chin, and cheeks caused by blocked oil glands. They are an expected finding that disappears within a few weeks without treatment, and squeezing them can injure the skin. Calling them whiteheads is tempting because they look like adult acne, but newborn skin absorbs products easily and does not need acne treatment. The nurse's role is to recognize the normal finding and reassure the parent.
questions.takeaway: Milia are harmless newborn white bumps: do not squeeze; they fade in a few weeks.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Think about how this finding could be misread later and how to prevent that.
questions.hintStrategy: When a normal finding could later be confused with an abnormal one, the best action is accurate documentation.
questions.stem: During the admission assessment of a 1-day-old with dark brown skin, the nurse notes several flat, blue-gray patches over the lower back and buttocks. Which action is most important for the nurse to take?
options: Report the patches to the provider as possible bruising from a difficult birth
Reassure the parents that these birthmarks are harmless and need no follow-up
Document the size, color, and location of the patches in the newborn's record
Ask the parents whether other family members had similar birthmarks as babies
optionRationales: Incorrect. Flat blue-gray patches in this location are a common birthmark in darker-skinned infants, not bruising.
Incorrect. Reassurance is accurate, but without documentation the patches could later be mistaken for bruises.
Correct. Blue-gray patches over the lower back and buttocks are expected birthmarks, and documenting them at birth keeps them from being mistaken later for bruises.
Incorrect. Family history is reasonable to ask, but it does not create the record that protects the family from a later false concern about abuse.
questions.rationale: Flat blue-gray patches over the lower back and buttocks are common birthmarks, especially in darker-skinned infants. They are expected and harmless, but because they look like bruises, the nurse documents their size, color, and location at birth. That record protects the family from a later false concern about abuse. Reporting them as bruising is the tempting answer for a student who is alert to injury, but these patches are present from birth and are flat and uniform.
questions.takeaway: Blue-gray patches over the lower back and buttocks are expected birthmarks: document size and location at birth so they are not later mistaken for bruises.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Pay attention to the order of events: when did the rash appear relative to the fever?
questions.hintStrategy: Match the timeline in the stem to the classic pattern of each childhood rash.
questions.stem: A parent calls about a 14-month-old who had a fever up to 39.8 °C (103.6 °F) for 4 days. Today the fever is gone, the child is drinking well and playing, and a pink rash has appeared on the trunk. The parent asks whether the rash means the child is getting worse. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “This sounds like fifth disease, a mild viral illness that will fade without treatment.”
“A pink trunk rash that appears as a high fever breaks is typical of roseola, a viral illness.”
“A rash after days of fever means a bacterial infection, so go to the emergency department.”
“A rash with a fever can mean measles, so keep the child away from others until seen.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The reassurance is fitting, but fifth disease starts with bright red cheeks in a mildly ill child, not a trunk rash after days of high fever.
Correct. Roseola causes several days of high fever followed by a pink rash on the trunk as the fever breaks, most often in infants and toddlers.
Incorrect. A child who is afebrile, drinking well, and playful with this classic pattern does not need emergency care.
Incorrect. Isolation is right for suspected measles, but measles rash starts on the face while fever continues; this rash appeared as the fever broke.
questions.rationale: Roseola is a viral illness of young children: 3 to 5 days of high fever, then a pink rash on the trunk appears as the fever breaks. A rash appearing as the child improves is part of the expected course, not a sign of worsening. The nurse reassures the parent and reinforces fluids and fever monitoring. The emergency-department option is tempting because rash plus fever can be serious, but red flags would be poor feeding, lethargy, or a rash with ongoing fever, which this child does not have.
questions.takeaway: High fever for several days, then a pink trunk rash as the fever breaks = roseola.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Look beyond the rash to how each child is eating, acting, and whether there is fever.
questions.hintStrategy: In triage items, eliminate the classic benign patterns, then choose the client with signs of systemic illness.

rows: Red blotches with small white-yellow centers on the chest and arms that come and go; breastfeeding well
New rash on the trunk; temperature 38.3 °C (100.9 °F); fed only twice in the past 8 hours; hard to wake
Bright red cheeks and a lacy pink rash on the arms after a mild cold last week; afebrile and playing
One large oval patch on the chest 10 days ago, now many small oval patches on the trunk; feels well

questions.stem: The pediatric clinic nurse reviews the triage log in the exhibit. Which client should the nurse contact first?
options: The 3-week-old
The 2-day-old
The 6-year-old
The 15-year-old
optionRationales: Correct. A rash with fever, poor feeding, and difficulty waking in a young infant is a red flag that needs prompt evaluation.
Incorrect. Red blotches with white-yellow centers that come and go in a well-feeding 2-day-old describe erythema toxicum, a harmless newborn rash.
Incorrect. Slapped cheeks and a lacy rash in a well child describe fifth disease, a mild viral illness.
Incorrect. A herald patch followed by smaller oval patches describes pityriasis rosea, which is harmless.
questions.rationale: Many childhood rashes are expected and harmless, so the nurse must pick out the one that is not. A rash in a newborn or young child that comes with fever, poor feeding, or lethargy must be reported promptly, and a 3-week-old with all three is the most at risk. Erythema toxicum, fifth disease, and pityriasis rosea are all benign patterns in children who are feeding or playing normally. The 2-day-old is tempting because it is the youngest, but its findings are the classic picture of a normal newborn rash.
questions.takeaway: A rash is not the problem; a rash with fever, poor feeding, or lethargy in an infant is the red flag.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Recall the pattern and course of the rash that begins with one larger patch.
questions.hintStrategy: When a diagnosis is benign and self-limiting, the correct teaching usually reassures and avoids unnecessary treatment.
questions.stem: A 17-year-old reports a single 4-cm oval pink patch on the chest that appeared 10 days ago, followed by many smaller oval patches across the trunk. The teen feels well. The provider diagnoses pityriasis rosea. Which teaching by the nurse is appropriate?
options: “Apply an antifungal cream to the patches twice a day until they clear.”
“Stay home from school until the patches fade so others do not catch it.”
“This rash is harmless and usually fades on its own over several weeks.”
“Call the clinic if the patches have not faded within the next week.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A single oval patch can look like ringworm, but the herald patch followed by many small patches identifies pityriasis rosea, which is not fungal.
Incorrect. Staying home sounds cautious, but pityriasis rosea is harmless and a teen who feels well does not need to miss school.
Correct. Pityriasis rosea is a harmless rash that fades on its own over several weeks.
Incorrect. Follow-up teaching is reasonable, but the rash normally lasts several weeks, so a one-week deadline would cause needless worry.
questions.rationale: Pityriasis rosea begins with one larger oval "herald patch," followed by many smaller oval patches on the trunk. It is harmless and fades on its own over several weeks, so teaching focuses on reassurance. The antifungal option is tempting because a single oval patch can resemble ringworm, but the pattern of a herald patch followed by many small patches identifies pityriasis rosea. Knowing which rashes are self-limiting prevents unnecessary worry and treatment.
questions.takeaway: Herald patch, then smaller oval patches on the trunk = pityriasis rosea, a harmless rash that fades in several weeks.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Consider the two main effects of thin newborn skin.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it adds heat loss or product absorption; those are the incorrect ones.
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching about skin care for the parents of a healthy full-term newborn. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid squeezing the tiny white bumps on the nose and chin
Use lotions, soaps, and creams sparingly and only as directed
Keep the newborn dry and dressed or covered to prevent heat loss
Rub an adult medicated cream on any rash to clear it quickly
Apply lotion over the whole body several times a day
Let any vernix left in the skin folds absorb on its own
optionRationales: Correct. These are milia, which go away on their own and should not be squeezed.
Correct. Newborn skin absorbs substances easily, so products are used sparingly and as directed.
Correct. Thin newborn skin loses heat quickly, so keeping the newborn dry and covered prevents heat loss.
Incorrect. Medicated creams can be absorbed through thin newborn skin and should be used only if prescribed for the newborn.
Incorrect. Frequent, whole-body lotion increases absorption and is not needed.
Correct. Vernix protects and moisturizes the skin and is absorbed on its own.
questions.rationale: Newborn skin is thin, so it loses heat quickly and absorbs substances easily. Teaching therefore stresses keeping the newborn dry and covered, using products sparingly, leaving vernix in place, and not squeezing milia. Applying lotion "to protect the skin" sounds caring and is the most tempting wrong option, but frequent whole-body products increase what the newborn absorbs. Adult medicated creams carry the greatest risk.
questions.takeaway: Newborn skin: keep warm and dry, use products sparingly, leave vernix and milia alone.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Think about how a child's skin surface compared with body weight affects fluid balance.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the assessment that detects the most immediate physiological threat, not the most visible finding.
questions.stem: A 3-year-old with widespread varicella lesions has had a fever of 39 °C (102.2 °F) for 2 days and has taken only a few sips of fluid today. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?
options: Hydration status, such as urine output, mucous membranes, and fluid intake
The number of new vesicles that have formed on the trunk since yesterday
The child's immunization record to see whether the varicella vaccine was given
Whether any brothers or sisters at home have already had chickenpox
optionRationales: Correct. Children have a larger body surface area for their weight, so fever and a widespread rash cause faster fluid loss, and this child is drinking little.
Incorrect. Counting new lesions tracks the illness but does not address the immediate risk of dehydration.
Incorrect. Vaccine history is useful information but does not change the urgent need to assess fluid status.
Incorrect. Sibling exposure matters for infection control but is not the priority physical assessment.
questions.rationale: Compared with their body weight, children have more skin surface, so they lose fluid and heat faster than adults, especially with fever, burns, or large rashes. This child has fever, widespread lesions, and poor intake, which together create a high risk of dehydration. Assessing urine output, mucous membranes, and intake addresses the most immediate physiological threat. Counting vesicles is tempting because the rash is the most visible problem, but the hidden fluid loss is more dangerous.
questions.takeaway: Larger body surface area means children dehydrate faster with fever or widespread rashes; assess hydration first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Separate changes caused by time and hormones from changes caused by outside exposures.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask of each option, "Would sunscreen or not smoking have changed this?"
questions.stem: A 56-year-old client who has smoked for 30 years and worked outdoors without sun protection asks which skin changes better habits might have prevented. Which changes are mainly the result of extrinsic aging? Select all that apply.
options: Deep wrinkles on the sun-exposed face and neck
Thinner, drier skin that developed after menopause
Rough, scaly precancerous patches on the backs of the hands
Leathery, thickened skin on the face and neck
Slower shedding of old skin cells that began in the client's 20s
Gradual loss of fat cells in the skin over time
optionRationales: Correct. UV exposure and smoking cause wrinkling on exposed skin.
Incorrect. Thinner, drier skin from lower estrogen after menopause is intrinsic aging.
Correct. Precancerous changes are caused by outside factors such as UV exposure.
Correct. UV light and smoking cause skin thickening, a sign of extrinsic aging.
Incorrect. Slower exfoliation beginning around age 20 is intrinsic aging.
Incorrect. Loss of fat cells is part of intrinsic aging.
questions.rationale: Intrinsic aging comes from genes and time: beginning around age 20, exfoliation slows and the skin holds less moisture and has fewer fat cells, collagen drops in the 40s, and estrogen loss at menopause thins and dries the skin. Extrinsic aging comes from outside factors such as UV light, pollution, smoking, and chemicals, and it causes thickening, precancerous changes, and wrinkling. Wrinkles can be tempting to classify as purely intrinsic, but deep wrinkling of sun-exposed skin in a smoker is largely extrinsic. Much of extrinsic aging is preventable with sun protection and not smoking.
questions.takeaway: Extrinsic aging (UV, smoking, pollution, chemicals) causes leathery thickening, wrinkles, and precancerous changes, and much of it is preventable.

questions.hintContent: Decide which findings are expected in pregnancy and what makes facial patches worse.
questions.hintStrategy: When the findings are normal, the best answer is usually the teaching that prevents them from getting worse.
questions.stem: A client at 24 weeks' gestation who works as a mail carrier notices a dark line down the middle of her abdomen, darker nipples, and new brown patches on her cheeks and forehead. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
options: Expect the patches to fade after delivery, so no special care is needed now
Report the dark line on the abdomen to the provider as soon as possible
Apply a fragrance-free moisturizer to the facial patches twice a day
Use sunscreen and a wide-brimmed hat to keep the facial patches from darkening
optionRationales: Incorrect. Melasma often fades after delivery, but sun exposure makes it darker now, especially for a client who works outdoors.
Incorrect. A dark line down the middle of the abdomen is an expected change of pregnancy.
Incorrect. Gentle moisturizing is safe, but it does not prevent the sun from darkening the patches.
Correct. Facial hyperpigmentation (melasma) is common in pregnancy, and sun protection helps keep the patches from getting darker.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy hormones commonly cause hyperpigmentation: a dark line down the abdomen, darker nipples, and darker patches on the face (melasma). These are expected changes, and sun exposure makes the facial patches darker, which matters for a client who works outdoors. Sun protection is the key teaching. Reporting the abdominal line is tempting for a cautious student, but it is a normal pregnancy finding.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy hyperpigmentation is expected; sun protection keeps facial patches from darkening.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Separate pigment and stretch changes caused by hormones from lesions that are warning signs at any age.
questions.hintStrategy: In "expected findings" SATA, remove anything that would be a red flag in a non-pregnant client.
questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks' gestation has several skin findings at a prenatal visit. Which findings are expected skin changes of pregnancy? Select all that apply.
options: Darkening of the skin of the nipples
A mole on the back that has darkened and bled this month
A dark line running down the middle of the abdomen
Itching of the abdominal skin as it stretches
Pink and purple stretch marks on the abdomen and thighs
A sore on the lower lip that has not healed in 2 months
optionRationales: Correct. Darker nipples are part of normal pregnancy hyperpigmentation.
Incorrect. A changing, bleeding mole is a warning sign at any age and needs evaluation.
Correct. A dark midline abdominal line is common pregnancy hyperpigmentation.
Correct. Itching from stretching and dry skin is common in pregnancy.
Correct. Stretch marks on the abdomen, breasts, and thighs are expected as the skin stretches.
Incorrect. A sore that does not heal needs evaluation and is not a pregnancy change.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy hormones cause expected skin changes: hyperpigmentation (a dark abdominal line, darker nipples, facial patches), stretch marks, and itching from stretching and dry skin. These can be reassured and managed with moisturizers and sun protection. A mole that is changing or bleeding and a sore that does not heal are red flags at every age, so pregnancy should never be used to explain them away. The darkened mole is tempting because pigment darkens in pregnancy, but bleeding and change point to possible melanoma.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy causes hyperpigmentation, stretch marks, and itching; a changing mole or non-healing sore is never "just pregnancy."

questions.hintContent: Recall which glands become more active at puberty.
questions.hintStrategy: Check that each option applies to the right age group; true facts about a different age are still wrong.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old wrestler has new acne on his back and a fungal rash between his toes. His parent asks why these problems started this year. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Sweaty gear and close skin contact on the wrestling mat can spread fungus to the feet.”
“Puberty hormones increase oil and sweat, which makes acne and fungal infections more common.”
“Stress from school and sports can trigger acne flares in many teens your son's age.”
“Showering right after every practice is the best way to prevent both of these problems.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Shared gear and skin contact do spread fungal infections, but this explains only the toe rash, not the new acne or why problems began at this age.
Correct. At puberty, hormones increase sebum and sweating, which explains both the acne and the fungal rash and why they began at this age.
Incorrect. Stress can worsen acne, but it is a secondary trigger and does not explain the fungal rash or the underlying hormonal change of puberty.
Incorrect. Showering after practice is good prevention teaching, but it does not answer the parent's question about why these problems started this year.
questions.rationale: At puberty, hormones increase sebum (oil) production and sweating. Extra oil helps plug follicles and cause acne, and sweat and moisture let fungi grow, so adolescents commonly have acne, dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal infections, and warts. A wrestler also has skin-to-skin contact and sweaty gear, which adds to the risk. The shared-gear option is tempting because it is true, but it explains only the fungal rash, while puberty hormones explain both problems and their timing.
questions.takeaway: Puberty hormones increase oil and sweat, so acne and fungal infections become common in adolescents.
