questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Identify which action creates friction on fragile skin.
questions.hintStrategy: "Requires intervention" means find the unsafe action; the correct actions are the distractors.
questions.stem: An RN observes a UAP providing morning care to an 88-year-old resident with thin, translucent skin. Which action by the UAP requires the RN to intervene?
options: Padding the wheelchair arms and leg rests with soft covers
Pulling the resident up in bed by sliding her across the sheet
Using lukewarm water and a mild cleanser for her bath
Putting a long-sleeved shirt on her to protect her forearms
optionRationales: Incorrect. Padding prevents bumps that can tear or bruise fragile skin.
Correct. Sliding creates friction and shear that can tear fragile skin; the UAP should lift with a draw sheet or lift device.
Incorrect. Lukewarm water and a mild cleanser protect dry, fragile skin.
Incorrect. Long sleeves protect the forearms from tears and bruises.
questions.rationale: With age, the dermis loses collagen and elastic fibers, so the skin is thin and tears or bruises easily. Safe care follows the rule "lift, don't drag": use a draw sheet or lift to reposition, pad equipment, protect the forearms, avoid tape, and use lukewarm water with mild cleansers. Sliding the resident across the sheet creates friction that can cause skin tears. The other actions are correct, so the RN supervises by stopping the unsafe one and showing the correct technique.
questions.takeaway: Fragile older skin: lift, don't drag; pad, don't tape; pat, don't rub; lukewarm, not hot.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Think about which skin layer provides insulation and how it changes with age.
questions.hintStrategy: For aging questions, check the direction of each change (increase or decrease); reversed directions are common distractors.
questions.stem: An 87-year-old resident often asks for an extra blanket and says, “I'm always cold, even when everyone else is warm.” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “With age, the skin makes less oil, so it often becomes dry, flaky, and itchy.”
“Older skin has fewer sweat glands, so you may overheat easily in hot weather.”
“With age, the skin becomes thinner, so it tears and bruises much more easily.”
“With age, the fat layer under the skin thins, so the body holds heat less well.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reduced oil production is a real aging change, but it causes dry skin, not a constant feeling of cold.
Incorrect. Fewer sweat glands is a true aging change that raises heat risk, but it does not explain why the resident always feels cold.
Incorrect. Thinner skin is a true aging change, but it explains tears and bruising rather than poor heat retention.
Correct. Loss of subcutaneous fat reduces insulation, and aging skin regulates temperature less well.
questions.rationale: Subcutaneous fat insulates the body, and it decreases with age. Combined with reduced temperature regulation, this makes older adults feel cold and puts them at risk for low body temperature. The other options describe real aging changes (less oil, fewer sweat glands, thinner skin), but each explains a different problem. Students who recognize a true aging fact may pick it without checking whether it answers the question asked.
questions.takeaway: Older adults feel cold because subcutaneous fat (insulation) decreases and temperature regulation declines.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Consider which functional skin changes make heat dangerous for older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client describes an unsafe practice, choose the response that explains the risk rather than one that modifies the unsafe practice.
questions.stem: A 79-year-old who lives alone tells the home health nurse, “My legs ache at night, so I sleep with a heating pad set on high under my calves.” Which response by the nurse is most important?
options: “Aging skin senses heat less, so you could be burned without feeling it.”
“A warm bath before bed may help ease the aching in your legs at night.”
“Use the pad on high only for the first few hours, then turn it off.”
“Mention the night leg aches to your provider at your next checkup visit.”
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults have decreased sensation and thin skin, so a heating pad can burn the skin before the client feels pain.
Incorrect. A warm bath is a reasonable comfort measure, but it does not address the immediate burn risk of the heating pad the client is using now.
Incorrect. Limiting the time sounds like a safe compromise, but it still relies on heat sensation the client may not have, so a burn can occur within hours.
Incorrect. Night leg aches do deserve evaluation, but this is not urgent, and the burn risk from tonight's heating pad use must be addressed first.
questions.rationale: Aging reduces sensation, so older adults may not feel pressure, heat, or injury, and their thin skin is injured more easily and heals more slowly. A heating pad on high for hours under the calves is a real burn risk. The nurse should explain the risk and help the client find a safer way to manage the leg aches. Limiting the time is tempting as a compromise, but it still relies on sensation the client may not have.
questions.takeaway: Decreased sensation in older adults means heat can burn before they feel it; avoid heating pads on high.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Consider where active children usually bruise and what multiple colors suggest about timing.
questions.hintStrategy: When abuse is suspected, choose objective documentation and reporting over confrontation or reassurance.
questions.stem: A 4-year-old is brought to the emergency department after a reported fall off the couch. The nurse notes purple, green, and yellow bruises on the buttocks, upper inner arms, and trunk. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the parent to explain why the bruises do not match the story of the fall
Apply cool compresses and teach the parent how to make the couch area safer
Document the findings objectively and report them according to facility policy
Ask the provider to order clotting studies to explain the easy bruising
optionRationales: Incorrect. The story does not fit, but confronting the parent can put the child at greater risk; the nurse documents and reports without needing proof.
Incorrect. Comfort and safety teaching are reasonable for an accidental injury, but this pattern suggests abuse and must be reported, not treated as a fall.
Correct. Bruises in different stages of healing in protected areas that do not match the history are possible signs of abuse and must be documented objectively and reported.
Incorrect. A bleeding disorder may be ruled out during the workup, but bruises in protected areas at different stages require a report now; lab tests do not replace it.
questions.rationale: Bruises in different stages of healing (purple, green, yellow), in protected areas such as the inner arms, trunk, and buttocks, or that do not match the story are possible signs of abuse at any age. Nurses are mandated reporters, so the nurse documents objectively and reports according to policy without needing proof. Confronting the parent is tempting because the story does not fit, but it can put the child at greater risk. Testing for a bleeding disorder may be part of the workup, but it does not replace the nurse's duty to report.
questions.takeaway: Bruises in different stages, in protected areas, or that do not match the story: document objectively and report per policy.

questions.hintContent: Separate expected aging changes from findings that suggest abuse, cancer, or infection.
questions.hintStrategy: In "requires follow-up" SATA, first label each finding as expected or unexpected for the client's age.

rows: Flat purple patches; client does not recall bumping them
Oval bruises in a row on both arms, in a fingertip-like pattern
Scattered flat brown age spots, unchanged for years per the client
Crusted sore present for 3 months that bleeds when touched
Skin tear with spreading redness, warmth, and cloudy drainage
Dry, flaky skin with mild itching

questions.stem: The home health nurse completes a skin assessment on an 85-year-old client who lives with an adult grandson. Refer to the exhibit. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Skin tear on the right shin with spreading redness and drainage
Flat purple patches on the forearms and hands
Fingertip-pattern bruises on both upper inner arms
Crusted, bleeding sore on the left ear present for 3 months
Dry, flaky skin on both lower legs
Unchanged brown age spots on the face and hands
optionRationales: Correct. Spreading redness, warmth, and drainage suggest an infected skin tear.
Incorrect. Flat purple patches on the forearms and hands are senile purpura, an expected finding from fragile vessels.
Correct. Fingertip-pattern bruises in a protected area are a possible sign of abuse and must be documented and reported.
Correct. A sore that bleeds and does not heal needs evaluation for possible skin cancer.
Incorrect. Dry, flaky skin is an expected aging change managed with moisturizer and gentle bathing.
Incorrect. Unchanged age spots are usually harmless; only changing spots need evaluation.
questions.rationale: In older adults, thin skin, senile purpura on the forearms and hands, stable age spots, and dry skin are expected changes. The nurse's job is to pick out what is not normal: bruises in a pattern or in protected areas (possible abuse), a sore that does not heal (possible skin cancer), and signs of infection in a skin tear. Senile purpura is the most tempting wrong choice because it looks like bruising, but its location on the forearms and backs of the hands and its flat appearance are typical of fragile aging vessels. Patterned bruises on the inner arms are different and must be reported.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, senile purpura and stable age spots are expected; patterned bruises, non-healing sores, and infected tears are not.

questions.hintContent: Compare each lab result with its reference range and link it to the resident's intake.
questions.hintStrategy: When an exhibit includes several labs, normal values are usually distractors; look for the one abnormal value that fits the problem.

rows: 86-year-old resident; 3-cm skin tear on the left forearm after bumping a doorframe; thin, translucent skin; senile purpura on both forearms.
Skin tear edges still open with little new tissue; no redness or drainage; eats about 25% of meals; afebrile.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the record of a long-term care resident whose skin tear is healing slowly. Refer to the exhibit. Which finding best explains the delayed healing?
options: Senile purpura on both forearms
Hemoglobin of 12.6 g/dL
WBC of 7,800/mm³
Albumin of 2.8 g/dL
optionRationales: Incorrect. Senile purpura is an expected aging finding from fragile vessels and does not explain slow healing.
Incorrect. The hemoglobin is within the normal range, so oxygen delivery is adequate.
Incorrect. The WBC is normal, and there are no signs of infection.
Correct. Albumin below 3.5 g/dL signals poor nutrition, which delays healing, and it matches the resident's 25% meal intake.
questions.rationale: Older adults heal more slowly, but poor nutrition makes healing much slower. An albumin below 3.5 g/dL, together with eating about 25% of meals, signals inadequate protein for building new tissue. The nurse reports the finding and supports protein, calories, vitamins A and C, and fluids. Senile purpura is tempting because it is a visible skin finding on the same arm, but it is an expected aging change, and the normal hemoglobin, WBC, and glucose are distractors.
questions.takeaway: Albumin below 3.5 g/dL with poor intake explains slow healing in an older adult; report it and improve nutrition.

questions.hintContent: Compare where irritant diaper rash appears with where this rash appears.
questions.hintStrategy: When standard care has failed and the pattern differs from the expected one, choose the action that escalates to the provider.
questions.stem: A 9-month-old has a diaper rash that the parent has treated with frequent changes and a barrier cream for 5 days without improvement. The nurse notes beefy red skin deep in the skin folds with small red satellite spots around the edges. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Tell the parent to keep using the barrier cream and frequent changes
Teach the parent to leave the diaper area open to air several times a day
Report the findings to the provider because an antifungal may be needed
Teach the parent to rinse with warm water instead of using baby wipes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Barrier cream and frequent changes are correct for ordinary diaper rash, but 5 days without improvement and satellite spots point to yeast.
Incorrect. Air exposure helps keep the skin dry and is good diaper care, but it will not clear a yeast infection that needs an antifungal.
Correct. Beefy red skin in the folds with satellite spots suggests a yeast (Candida) diaper rash, which needs an antifungal.
Incorrect. Gentle rinsing reduces irritation and is good teaching, but it does not treat the Candida infection this pattern suggests.
questions.rationale: Irritant diaper dermatitis from urine and stool causes red, shiny skin where the diaper touches, while the deep skin folds are usually spared. A rash that is beefy red in the skin folds with small satellite spots suggests a yeast (Candida) infection, which needs an antifungal and should be reported. Continuing the barrier cream is tempting because it is the correct care for ordinary diaper rash, but this pattern and the lack of improvement point to a different cause. Recognizing the pattern directs the right treatment.
questions.takeaway: Diaper rash in the folds with satellite spots = suspect yeast; report for an antifungal.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Identify what causes irritant diaper dermatitis and how to limit skin contact with it.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option by whether it keeps the skin clean and dry without adding friction or irritants.
questions.stem: The parent of a 4-month-old with a stomach virus and frequent loose stools asks how to prevent diaper rash. Which instructions should the nurse give? Select all that apply.
options: Use scented wipes and scrub until all residue is gone
Apply a barrier cream if the provider recommends one
Fasten the diaper tightly so stool cannot leak onto other skin
Let the skin air-dry before putting on a clean diaper
Change the diaper as soon as it is wet or soiled
Clean the skin gently with warm water or a mild cleanser
optionRationales: Incorrect. Fragrance and scrubbing irritate already stressed skin.
Correct. A barrier cream protects the skin from urine and stool when recommended.
Incorrect. A tight diaper traps moisture and increases friction.
Correct. Air-drying keeps the skin dry before the next diaper goes on.
Correct. Frequent changes limit the time urine and stool stay on the skin.
Correct. Gentle cleaning removes irritants without damaging the skin.
questions.rationale: Diaper dermatitis is an irritant dermatitis: urine and stool sitting on the skin, especially with diarrhea, damage the barrier. Prevention keeps the skin clean and dry with frequent changes, gentle cleaning, air-drying, and a barrier cream when recommended. A tight diaper is the tempting wrong answer because it seems to contain the mess, but it traps moisture and rubs the skin. Scented wipes and scrubbing add irritants and friction.
questions.takeaway: Diaper rash prevention: change often, clean gently, air-dry, and use a barrier cream if recommended.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens to fragile skin when adhesive is pulled off.
questions.hintStrategy: In "needs further teaching" items, find the one statement that could cause harm.
questions.stem: The home health nurse taught the adult daughter of an 87-year-old with fragile skin and senile purpura how to protect her father's skin. Which statement by the daughter indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I'll give him a bath every other day using lukewarm water and a mild soap.”
“I'll hold the dressing on his arm in place with strips of adhesive tape.”
“I'll use a draw sheet to move him up in bed instead of pulling him.”
“I'll put moisturizer on him right after his bath while he's still damp.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Bathing every other day with lukewarm water is recommended for older adults.
Correct. This statement needs correction: adhesive tape can tear fragile skin when removed, so gauze wraps or tape-free options are used.
Incorrect. Lifting with a draw sheet prevents friction and skin tears.
Incorrect. Moisturizing right after bathing while the skin is damp locks in water.
questions.rationale: Older adults have thin, fragile skin from loss of collagen and elastic fibers, so everyday care must avoid friction and trauma. The rules are lift, don't drag; pat, don't rub; pad, don't tape; and lukewarm, not hot, with bathing every other day and moisturizer afterward. Adhesive tape is the error because removing it can strip or tear the skin. The other statements show correct understanding.
questions.takeaway: Never use adhesive tape on fragile older skin; use gauze wraps or tape-free options.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Consider what causes newborn acne and what thin newborn skin does with products applied to it.
questions.hintStrategy: When a finding is normal for age, the best answer avoids treatment that adds risk.
questions.stem: The parent of a 3-week-old notices small red and white bumps on the infant's cheeks and says, “I'll put a little of my teenager's benzoyl peroxide gel on them.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Newborn acne fades on its own, and baby skin absorbs products easily, so skip the gel.”
“Wash the bumps twice a day with a mild baby soap, which will help clear them up.”
“Ask the baby's provider which acne cream is safe to use on a newborn's skin.”
“Those are milia, tiny blocked oil glands, and they will fade in a few weeks.”
optionRationales: Correct. Neonatal acne comes from the parent's hormones, resolves with gentle washing, and newborn skin absorbs products easily.
Incorrect. Gentle washing is appropriate care, but this response does not address the parent's plan to use benzoyl peroxide, which is the safety concern.
Incorrect. Checking with the provider sounds cautious, but neonatal acne needs no cream, and this response leaves the door open to an unneeded medicated product.
Incorrect. Milia also fade on their own, but they are tiny white bumps; red and white bumps at 3 weeks are neonatal acne, and this does not address the gel.
questions.rationale: Neonatal acne appears as small red or white bumps on a newborn's face and comes from the parent's hormones. It needs only gentle washing and goes away on its own. Newborn skin is thin and absorbs products easily, so adult or teen acne medicines should not be used. Advising gentle washing or asking the provider about a cream are tempting because they sound careful, but the priority is to stop the unneeded medicated product.
questions.takeaway: Neonatal acne resolves on its own; thin newborn skin absorbs products, so no acne medicines.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Label each finding as an expected aging change or a complication.
questions.hintStrategy: In "assess first" items, eliminate expected findings and choose the client with signs of a new complication.
questions.stem: The nurse in a long-term care facility receives reports about four residents. Which resident should the nurse assess first?
options: An 82-year-old with new flat purple patches on the backs of both hands
A 90-year-old with dry, flaky skin on both shins and mild itching
An 86-year-old whose forearm skin tear is red, warm, and draining cloudy fluid
A 79-year-old with several flat brown age spots on the face that are unchanged
optionRationales: Incorrect. Flat purple patches on the hands are senile purpura, an expected aging finding.
Incorrect. Dry, itchy skin is common with fewer oil glands and is managed with moisturizer.
Correct. Redness, warmth, and cloudy drainage in a skin tear suggest infection, which can spread in an older adult with slower healing.
Incorrect. Unchanged age spots are usually harmless.
questions.rationale: Older adults have many expected skin changes, including senile purpura, dry skin, and age spots. Signs of infection in a skin tear, such as spreading redness, warmth, swelling, and pus, are not expected and need prompt assessment, especially because older adults heal slowly and may show subtle signs of infection. The new purple patches are tempting because "new" sounds urgent, but flat purple patches on the hands are typical senile purpura. The nurse sees the resident with the possible infection first.
questions.takeaway: Among older adults, expected changes can wait; a skin tear with redness, warmth, and drainage is seen first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.hintContent: Consider the link between appearance and self-esteem in adolescence.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose responses that explore feelings and offer safe help; eliminate minimizing statements and unsafe advice.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old with moderate acne on his back tells the school nurse he has started skipping gym class because he does not want classmates to see his back in the locker room. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Advise him to squeeze the larger pimples so they heal faster
Tell him acne is just a phase that everyone grows out of
Suggest an online skin-bleaching product for the dark marks
Ask him how the acne is affecting the way he feels about himself
Discuss safe treatment options and a visit with his provider
Listen to his concerns without judging or minimizing them
optionRationales: Incorrect. Squeezing worsens inflammation and scarring.
Incorrect. Calling it a phase minimizes his feelings and closes the conversation.
Incorrect. Strong bleaching creams can irritate the skin or interact with medications.
Correct. Asking how the teen feels assesses the effect on self-esteem, which is closely tied to appearance in adolescence.
Correct. Offering safe treatment options addresses the problem behind the avoidance.
Correct. Listening without judgment builds trust and encourages the teen to share.
questions.rationale: Acne affects about 85% of people aged 12 to 24, and for teens appearance is closely tied to self-esteem. Skin problems can lead to embarrassment, avoiding activities, or trying risky fixes. The nurse asks how the teen feels, listens without judging, and offers safe treatment options. Calling acne "just a phase" is tempting because it is common, but it dismisses the teen's distress.
questions.takeaway: For a teen upset about acne: ask about feelings, listen without judging, and offer safe treatment.

questions.hintContent: Link each teaching point to a specific age-related skin change.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option against the fragile-skin rules: lukewarm not hot, pat not rub, pad not tape.
questions.stem: An 81-year-old who lives alone has thin skin, reduced sensation in both feet, and senile purpura on the forearms. Which teaching points should the nurse include to protect the client's skin? Select all that apply.
options: Look at the feet and legs every day for injuries you may not feel
Check the bath water temperature with a thermometer or elbow first
Hold bandages on fragile skin with strips of adhesive tape
Pad sharp furniture corners and wear long sleeves around the house
Rub the skin briskly with a towel after bathing to help circulation
Take a hot bath every day with deodorant soap to stay clean
optionRationales: Correct. Daily inspection finds injuries the client cannot feel.
Correct. Reduced sensation means the client may not feel water that is hot enough to burn.
Incorrect. Adhesive tape can tear fragile skin; use gauze wraps or tape-free options.
Correct. Padding and long sleeves prevent skin tears and bruises.
Incorrect. Rubbing causes friction; pat the skin dry.
Incorrect. Hot water and harsh soap dry fragile skin; bathe every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser.
questions.rationale: Aging skin is thin, dry, and slow to heal, and reduced sensation means the client may not feel heat, pressure, or injury. Teaching for an older adult living alone emphasizes checking water temperature, inspecting the skin daily, padding and protecting the arms and legs, bathing every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser, patting dry, and avoiding tape. A daily hot bath is tempting because it sounds hygienic and comforting, but it strips oils and risks burns. Each correct point compensates for a specific age-related change.
questions.takeaway: For older adults with reduced sensation: test water temperature, inspect skin daily, pad and protect, and avoid hot water, rubbing, and tape.

questions.hintContent: Apply the ABCDE rule and recall which letter matters most.
questions.hintStrategy: In "refer first" items, look for change over time; a stable finding is rarely the priority.
questions.stem: At a community skin screening, the nurse assesses four clients. Which finding should the nurse refer for prompt provider evaluation?
options: A 3-mm mole on the shin that began to itch and crust last month
A round, evenly tan freckle on the nose that has not changed in years
Small, smooth dark bumps on the cheeks of a client with dark skin, present for years
Razor bumps along the beard line of a client who shaves every day
optionRationales: Correct. A mole that is changing or has new itching or crusting is "evolving," the most important melanoma warning sign, even when it is small.
Incorrect. A small, round, evenly colored spot that stays the same is typical of a benign lesion.
Incorrect. Small, smooth dark facial bumps that have been stable for years fit dermatosis papulosa nigra, a harmless condition more common in darker skin.
Incorrect. Razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis) are a common, benign problem from shaving.
questions.rationale: The ABCDE rule flags moles that may be melanoma, and E (evolving) matters most: a mole that changes, or starts to itch, crust, or bleed, needs evaluation even if it is smaller than 6 mm. Stable, evenly colored spots and common benign conditions of darker skin do not need urgent referral. The small size of the shin mole makes it tempting to dismiss, because many students remember only the "larger than a pencil eraser" rule. Change outranks size.
questions.takeaway: A mole that is changing, itching, crusting, or bleeding needs evaluation no matter how small it is.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.hintContent: Run each option through the ABCDE rule.
questions.hintStrategy: For SATA, judge each characteristic on its own; a single warning sign is enough to report.
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 45-year-old client with many moles how to recognize warning signs during monthly self-exams. Which mole characteristics should the client report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: A single even color that has stayed the same for years
One half of the mole does not match the other half
Edges that are ragged, notched, or blurred
A diameter of 3 mm with smooth, even borders
Several shades of brown and black within one mole
A small, round mole that has recently started to bleed
optionRationales: Incorrect. One even color that stays the same is a reassuring feature.
Correct. Asymmetry is the A in the ABCDE rule.
Correct. An irregular border is the B in the ABCDE rule.
Incorrect. A small mole with smooth, even borders is typical of a normal mole.
Correct. Varied color is the C in the ABCDE rule.
Correct. New bleeding is a sign of evolving (E), which needs evaluation regardless of size.
questions.rationale: A normal mole is usually small, round, evenly colored, and unchanged for years. The ABCDE rule flags moles that break these rules: Asymmetry, irregular Border, varied Color, Diameter larger than about 6 mm, and Evolving (any change in size, shape, color, or height, or new itching, crusting, or bleeding). The small bleeding mole is the most commonly missed warning sign because it fails the size test, but evolving is the most important letter. Stable, small, symmetric, evenly colored moles are reassuring.
questions.takeaway: ABCDE: asymmetry, irregular border, varied color, diameter over 6 mm, and evolving; any change means get it checked.

questions.hintContent: Recall which skin cancer is most common and which is most serious.
questions.hintStrategy: Watch for options that swap the key facts of two similar conditions.
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client has a pearly, waxy bump with tiny visible blood vessels on the side of the nose. The provider suspects basal cell carcinoma. The client asks, “Is this the kind of cancer that spreads all over?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “The biopsy will tell us the type, so it is too early to say anything about that.”
“Basal cell is the most common skin cancer, and many people are treated for it.”
“Any skin cancer can spread, so you will likely need a full-body scan quite soon.”
“Basal cell cancer grows slowly and rarely spreads, but it still needs to be treated.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The biopsy does confirm the type, but the provider already suspects basal cell carcinoma, and the nurse can give accurate information instead of avoiding the question.
Incorrect. This is true and may reassure, but it does not answer the client's question about whether the cancer spreads.
Incorrect. Basal cell carcinoma can spread in rare cases, but scans are not routine for it, and this response is alarming and inaccurate.
Correct. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer; it grows slowly and rarely spreads, but it still requires treatment.
questions.rationale: The three skin cancers are named for the cells they start in. Basal cell carcinoma starts in the deepest layer of the epidermis, often looks like a pearly or waxy bump with tiny visible vessels, is the most common type, grows slowly, and rarely spreads. Melanoma is the most serious type and can spread early. Confusing "most common" with "most serious" is the classic error, so the nurse gives an honest answer that is accurate without being alarming.
questions.takeaway: Basal cell = most common, slow-growing, rarely spreads; melanoma = most serious.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.hintContent: Match the lesion's appearance and the client's history to the three skin cancers.
questions.hintStrategy: Use every clue in the stem: duration, appearance, location, and related findings all point to one answer.
questions.stem: A 72-year-old retired commercial fisherman has a rough, scaly, crusted sore on the lower lip that bleeds easily and has been present for 2 months. He also has several rough pink patches on the tops of his ears. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: The sore is most likely a cold sore that will heal on its own within 2 weeks
The sore may be squamous cell carcinoma, which can spread and needs prompt evaluation
The sore is an expected change of aging skin in a client who worked outdoors
The sore is most likely melanoma because it is crusted and bleeds easily
optionRationales: Incorrect. The sore has lasted 2 months and is scaly and crusted, which does not fit a self-limited cold sore.
Correct. A rough, scaly, crusted sore on the lip that bleeds and does not heal fits squamous cell carcinoma, which can spread and often arises in sun-damaged skin with actinic keratoses.
Incorrect. A sore that bleeds and does not heal is never just aging and needs evaluation.
Incorrect. Melanoma usually appears as a changing, multicolored mole or dark spot, not a scaly crusted sore.
questions.rationale: Squamous cell carcinoma starts in the flat cells of the epidermis and appears as a rough, scaly, crusted bump or sore that may bleed, often on the face, lips, ears, and hands. It can spread and often develops from actinic keratoses, the rough pink patches caused by years of sun damage. Decades on the water gave this client heavy UV exposure. Melanoma is tempting because it is the cancer students remember best, but its appearance is a changing pigmented lesion rather than a scaly sore.
questions.takeaway: A rough, scaly, crusted sore that bleeds or will not heal on sun-exposed skin suggests squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.hintContent: Rank the results by how likely each is to spread.
questions.hintStrategy: When comparing diagnoses, prioritize the one with the greatest potential for rapid harm.
questions.stem: The nurse in a dermatology clinic reviews the biopsy results in the exhibit. Which client should the nurse call first to arrange a prompt follow-up appointment with the provider?
options: The 58-year-old
The 47-year-old
The 64-year-old
The 71-year-old
optionRationales: Incorrect. Basal cell carcinoma rarely spreads, and the margins are clear.
Correct. Malignant melanoma is the most serious skin cancer and can spread early to lymph nodes and organs.
Incorrect. Actinic keratosis is precancerous and needs follow-up, but it is not an active cancer.
Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma can spread, but this lesion was removed with clear margins.
questions.rationale: Of the three skin cancers, malignant melanoma is the most serious because it starts in the melanocytes and can spread early to lymph nodes and other organs, so it needs the fastest follow-up. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common but rarely spreads. Squamous cell carcinoma can spread, which makes it the most tempting distractor, but this lesion was removed with clear margins. Actinic keratosis is precancerous and is managed on a routine schedule.
questions.takeaway: Melanoma is the most serious skin cancer and gets the fastest follow-up.

questions.hintContent: Consider what a tan actually tells you about the skin cells.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that make an unsafe practice "safer"; choose the one that corrects the misconception.
questions.stem: A 17-year-old tells the school nurse, “I'm going to a tanning salon twice a week before spring break so I'll have a base tan and won't burn at the beach.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “If you do go, be sure to wear the goggles every time to protect your eyes.”
“Even with a base tan, wear SPF 30 sunscreen whenever you are at the beach.”
“Many states limit tanning bed use by teens because of the skin cancer risks.”
“A tan is a sign of skin damage, so a base tan won't protect you from skin cancer.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Goggles are a true safety measure, but this accepts the plan and does not correct the belief that a base tan protects the skin.
Incorrect. Sunscreen at the beach is correct teaching, but it is incomplete because it does not correct the base-tan misconception or discourage tanning beds.
Incorrect. This is true, but it does not explain why a base tan fails to protect, which is the misconception the teen needs corrected.
Correct. A tan means DNA damage has already happened, and tanning beds add UV exposure rather than protection.
questions.rationale: UV radiation from the sun or tanning beds damages the DNA of skin cells, and the damage adds up over years. A tan is the skin's response to damage that has already occurred, so a "base tan" is not protection. The nurse teaches no tanning beds and real sun protection: broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, reapplication, shade, and clothing. Advising goggles or beach sunscreen is tempting because each is true, but neither corrects the belief that drives the risky plan.
questions.takeaway: There is no safe tan: tanning beds and base tans add UV damage rather than protection.

questions.hintContent: Recall where melanoma is more often found in darker skin and which ABCDE sign is present.
questions.hintStrategy: Be wary of options that rely on skin tone to rule out cancer; those are almost always wrong.
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with dark brown skin mentions a dark brown streak under the big toenail that has become wider over the past few months. The client says, “I probably just stubbed it.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Recommend a prompt provider evaluation of the streak for possible melanoma
Reassure the client that dark streaks under the nails are normal in dark skin
Measure the streak's width today and recheck it at the next routine visit
Explain that a bruise from a stubbed toe can take months to grow out
optionRationales: Correct. In darker skin, melanoma is more often found under the nails and on the palms and soles, and a widening streak is evolving.
Incorrect. Even, stable nail streaks are common in darker skin, but a streak that is widening is evolving and is not normal.
Incorrect. Measuring the streak is useful assessment, but it is already known to be widening, and waiting for a routine visit delays diagnosis.
Incorrect. A stubbed toe can bruise the nail bed and take months to grow out, but a bruise does not widen over time, so this falsely reassures and delays evaluation.
questions.rationale: In darker skin, melanoma is more often found on the palms, soles, and under the nails, and it is often diagnosed later. A dark streak under a nail that is getting wider is evolving, the most important ABCDE warning sign, and needs prompt evaluation. Accepting the client's explanation of trauma is tempting, but an injury would not cause a streak to widen over months. All clients are at risk regardless of skin tone.
questions.takeaway: A changing dark streak under a nail needs evaluation for melanoma, especially in clients with darker skin.

questions.hintContent: Recall what melanin does for the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the condition's name to the structure it affects, then pick the explanation that follows from it.
questions.stem: A 9-year-old with albinism will attend an outdoor summer day camp. The parent asks why the child burns so much faster than the child's siblings. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Children's skin is thinner than adult skin, so it is easily damaged.”
“Albinism is inherited, so it runs in families and is present from birth.”
“Your child's skin makes little or no melanin, the pigment that absorbs UV light.”
“Albinism also affects the eyes, so your child is sensitive to bright light.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Children's skin is more delicate, but the siblings are children too, so this does not explain why this child burns faster.
Incorrect. Albinism is inherited, but this describes the cause of the condition, not why the skin burns so quickly.
Correct. Albinism is an inherited condition with little or no melanin, so the skin has almost no natural UV protection.
Incorrect. Light sensitivity of the eyes is true in albinism, but the parent asked about sunburn, which comes from missing melanin in the skin.
questions.rationale: Melanin is the pigment that absorbs UV radiation and protects skin cells from damage. In albinism, an inherited condition, the skin makes little or no melanin, so it has almost no natural UV protection and a very high risk of burns and skin cancer. The child needs strict sun protection: shade, clothing, a hat, sunglasses, and broad-spectrum sunscreen reapplied often. The other statements about albinism and children's skin are true, but only missing melanin explains the fast burning.
questions.takeaway: Albinism = little or no melanin = almost no natural UV protection; teach strict sun protection.

questions.hintContent: Identify the client's risk factors and recall how often self-exams should be done.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the option that is complete in both frequency and coverage.
questions.stem: A 45-year-old client has more than 50 moles and a sister who was treated for melanoma. Which skin cancer screening plan should the nurse recommend?
options: Monthly full-body self-exams, with no provider exam needed
A yearly full-skin exam by a provider, with no self-exams
Monthly self-exams of only moles larger than a pencil eraser
Monthly self-exams plus a yearly full-skin exam by a provider
optionRationales: Incorrect. Monthly whole-body self-exams are important, but a high-risk client also needs a yearly expert exam that can catch subtle changes.
Incorrect. A yearly provider exam is appropriate, but changes between visits can be missed without monthly self-exams.
Incorrect. Monthly self-exams are right, but evolving moles of any size need attention, and this client also needs a yearly provider exam.
Correct. A client with many moles and a family history of melanoma benefits from monthly self-exams and a yearly professional exam.
questions.rationale: Many moles and a family history of melanoma both raise risk, so this client needs regular screening. Monthly self-exams help the client learn what normal skin looks like and notice changes early, and a yearly full-skin exam by a provider adds an expert look and possible biopsy. Either one alone is incomplete for a high-risk client. Checking only large moles is tempting because of the 6-mm rule, but evolving moles of any size need attention, and self-exams should cover the whole body.
questions.takeaway: High-risk clients: monthly self-exams plus a yearly professional skin exam.

questions.hintContent: Run the mole through the ABCDE rule.
questions.hintStrategy: When an abnormal finding is discovered incidentally, choose documentation and reporting over waiting.
questions.stem: While bathing a 68-year-old client admitted for pneumonia, the nurse notices a 9-mm mole on the client's back with an irregular border and areas of black and red. The client says he has never seen it because he cannot see his back. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Wait until the pneumonia resolves, then recheck the mole at discharge
Recommend that he see a dermatologist after he is discharged
Document the mole's features and notify the provider for evaluation
Measure the mole and describe its features in the nursing notes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Treating the pneumonia is the admission focus, but reporting the mole does not interfere with that care, and waiting delays evaluation.
Incorrect. A dermatology referral is reasonable, but this mole meets several ABCDE criteria and should be reported to the provider during this admission.
Correct. The mole meets several ABCDE criteria (border, color, diameter), so it should be documented and reported for evaluation.
Incorrect. Measuring and documenting are needed, but this is incomplete because the provider must also be notified to evaluate the mole.
questions.rationale: A skin assessment during routine care is a chance to find skin cancer early. This mole shows an irregular Border, varied Color, and a Diameter over 6 mm, so it meets several ABCDE criteria and needs provider evaluation and possible biopsy. Melanoma can spread early, so the finding should be reported during this admission even though the client came in for another reason. Waiting until the pneumonia resolves is tempting because the acute illness feels like the focus, but documenting and reporting do not interfere with that care.
questions.takeaway: A mole meeting ABCDE criteria is documented and reported when found, even if the client was admitted for something else.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.hintContent: Count the risk factors each student has.
questions.hintStrategy: When all clients are at some risk, pick the one with the most and strongest risk factors.
questions.stem: The nurse at a college health fair has time to give in-depth skin cancer prevention teaching to one more student today. Which student is at highest risk and should be selected?
options: A student with dark brown skin who works in the campus library and wears a hat outdoors
A fair-skinned student with red hair who uses tanning beds and had blistering sunburns as a child
A student with medium skin who wears SPF 30 sunscreen daily and avoids the midday sun
A student with olive skin who had one mild sunburn last summer and has a few small moles
optionRationales: Incorrect. All skin tones are at risk, but this student has more melanin and limited sun exposure.
Correct. Light skin, tanning-bed use, and blistering sunburns in childhood each raise skin cancer risk, and this student has all three.
Incorrect. This student already practices sun protection.
Incorrect. One mild sunburn and a few small moles add some risk, but less than the first student.
questions.rationale: Lighter skin has less melanin, so it is more easily damaged by UV light. Tanning-bed use and blistering sunburns in childhood add to that risk because UV damage to skin cells builds up over time. Every client is at risk regardless of skin tone, but when time is limited, the nurse focuses teaching on the client with the most risk factors. The olive-skinned student is tempting because of the moles, but that student has fewer and milder risk factors.
questions.takeaway: Light skin, tanning beds, and blistering sunburns stack up; the client with the most risk factors gets priority teaching.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Consider who is responsible for assessment and what information the provider will need.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act or report, unless the situation is a life-threatening emergency.
questions.stem: A UAP reports to the RN that while bathing a 76-year-old resident, she noticed a dark mole on the resident's shoulder that bled when she washed over it. Which action should the RN take first?
options: Go to the resident and assess the mole's size, shape, border, and color
Notify the provider right away that the UAP has found a bleeding mole
Instruct the UAP to cover the mole and check it again during the next bath
Document the UAP's report of a bleeding mole in the resident's record
optionRationales: Correct. The RN assesses the finding personally before acting on it, gathering ABCDE data to report accurately.
Incorrect. The provider should be notified, but only after the RN has assessed the mole and can give complete information.
Incorrect. Monitoring is not delegated, and a bleeding mole needs assessment now.
Incorrect. Documentation follows the RN's own assessment.
questions.rationale: A mole that bleeds is a possible evolving lesion and needs evaluation. UAPs can report what they observe, but assessment belongs to the RN, so the RN first assesses the mole personally using the ABCDE features. That assessment provides the information the provider needs. Notifying the provider immediately is tempting because the finding is concerning, but the call is more useful once the RN has assessed the lesion.
questions.takeaway: When a UAP reports an abnormal finding, the RN assesses it personally before notifying the provider.

questions.hintContent: Recall the SPF level, the spectrum, and how often sunscreen must be reapplied.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each option for a hidden myth: "lasts all day," "base tan," or "clouds block UV."
questions.stem: A 22-year-old with fair skin and red hair is starting a summer job as a landscaper. Which instruction about sun protection is most appropriate?
options: Apply SPF 50 once in the morning, since a higher SPF lasts through the whole day
Wear a wide-brimmed hat and long sleeves instead of using sunscreen at work
Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher before work and reapply about every 2 hours
Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher each morning before starting work
optionRationales: Incorrect. A higher SPF does block more UVB, but no sunscreen lasts all day; sweat and time wear it off, so reapplication is needed.
Incorrect. Hats and sleeves are important protection, but they leave the face, neck, and hands exposed, so sunscreen is still needed.
Correct. Broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, reapplied about every 2 hours and after sweating, is the standard recommendation.
Incorrect. This product and timing are correct, but it is incomplete because sunscreen must be reapplied about every 2 hours during outdoor work.
questions.rationale: Sun protection is the most important way to prevent skin cancer, and this client has light skin and long hours of outdoor work. Sunscreen should be broad-spectrum (UVA and UVB), SPF 30 or higher, and reapplied about every 2 hours and after sweating or towel drying, along with a wide-brimmed hat, long sleeves, and shade when possible. The SPF 50 option is tempting because a higher number sounds stronger, but no sunscreen lasts all day. Clothing helps but does not replace sunscreen on exposed skin.
questions.takeaway: Broad-spectrum SPF 30+, reapplied about every 2 hours and after sweating, every day including cloudy days.

questions.hintContent: Separate expected post-biopsy findings from a complication.
questions.hintStrategy: Physical threats come before psychosocial needs; choose the unexpected physical finding.
questions.stem: A client calls the dermatology clinic 6 hours after a biopsy of a pearly lesion on the forearm. Which report requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
options: “Blood has soaked through the bandage twice even though I pressed on it.”
“The biopsy site feels a little sore when I bump it against something.”
“There's a small spot of pink drainage on the bandage from this morning.”
“I'm nervous and want to know how soon the results will come back.”
optionRationales: Correct. Bleeding that soaks the dressing and does not stop with pressure must be reported and addressed now.
Incorrect. Mild soreness at a biopsy site is expected.
Incorrect. A small amount of pink drainage soon after a biopsy is expected.
Incorrect. The client's anxiety deserves a response, but it is not a physical threat.
questions.rationale: After a skin biopsy, the client keeps the site clean and covered and reports redness, swelling, drainage, or bleeding that will not stop. Bleeding that soaks through the bandage twice despite pressure is the one report that signals an active physical problem. Mild soreness and a small amount of pink drainage are expected. The anxious client is tempting because waiting for a possible cancer result is stressful, but a physical complication comes first.
questions.takeaway: After a skin biopsy, bleeding that will not stop with pressure needs immediate follow-up; mild soreness and scant drainage are expected.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.hintContent: Consider what melanin does and does not protect against.
questions.hintStrategy: Any option claiming a skin tone cannot be damaged by the sun is wrong.
questions.stem: A 29-year-old client with dark brown skin and melasma on both cheeks says, “I don't need sunscreen. People with my skin color don't get sun damage.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Your skin does have more natural protection, so a wide hat may be enough.”
“Many people believe that. What have you heard about sunscreen and dark skin?”
“A tinted moisturizer with sunscreen can help even out your melasma patches.”
“Darker skin can still be damaged by UV, and sun makes melasma patches darker.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Darker skin does have more melanin, but it is not immune to UV damage, and a hat alone does not protect all exposed skin.
Incorrect. Exploring the client's beliefs is a reasonable start, but this misconception affects health, so the nurse should give accurate information.
Incorrect. Sunscreen does help melasma, but this response does not correct the belief that darker skin is not damaged by the sun.
Correct. Darker skin has more melanin but is not immune to UV damage or skin cancer, and sun exposure worsens melasma.
questions.rationale: Darker skin has more melanin, which absorbs UV, but it is not immune to sun damage or skin cancer, and skin cancer in darker skin is often found later. Melasma, the dark facial patches more common in darker skin, gets darker with sun exposure, which gives this client a personal reason to use protection. Partly agreeing with the client is tempting because darker skin does have more natural protection, but "less risk" is not "no risk." Sun protection is for every skin tone.
questions.takeaway: Sun protection is for every skin tone; in darker skin, it also keeps melasma from darkening.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.hintContent: Think about how repeated UV exposure affects skin-cell DNA over a lifetime.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that put a time limit on risk; cumulative-damage questions reward the "adds up" answer.
questions.stem: A 61-year-old client says, “I had a lot of bad sunburns as a lifeguard when I was a teenager, but I haven't burned in 30 years, so that damage is behind me.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Protecting your skin now still matters, because new sun exposure adds to your risk.”
“Sun damage to skin cells adds up over the years, so skin cancer can appear decades later.”
“Most skin cancers can be cured when they are found and treated early enough.”
“A yearly skin exam by a provider will catch any problems from that old sun damage.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Ongoing sun protection is correct teaching, but this does not correct the belief that the old damage is behind him.
Correct. Each burn or tan adds DNA damage, and skin cancer often appears decades after the exposure.
Incorrect. Early detection does improve outcomes, but this does not answer whether his past burns still affect his risk.
Incorrect. A yearly exam is appropriate, but it does not explain that old damage persists and overpromises what one exam can catch.
questions.rationale: UV radiation damages the DNA of skin cells, and that damage builds up over years. Skin cancer often shows up decades after the burns and tans that caused it, which is why it appears most on sun-exposed skin in older adults. This client's history of repeated teenage burns raises risk now, so monthly self-exams, a yearly professional exam, and ongoing sun protection are appropriate. Statements about sun protection or screening are true, but only the cumulative-damage explanation corrects his belief.
questions.takeaway: UV damage accumulates; skin cancer can appear decades after the sunburns that caused it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.hintContent: Recall which risk factors for skin cancer cannot be changed.
questions.hintStrategy: Beware of "only" and "skips" in answer choices; risk factors usually add together.
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client says, “My father was just diagnosed with melanoma. Does that change anything for me?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Sun exposure is the main cause of melanoma, so focus on wearing sunscreen daily.”
“A parent with melanoma raises your own risk, so regular skin checks matter more.”
“Watch for any new or changing moles and report them to your provider promptly.”
“Your risk may be higher, so ask your provider about genetic testing for melanoma.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. UV is the main cause of skin cancer and sunscreen matters, but this ignores that family history also raises the client's risk.
Correct. A family history of melanoma raises a client's own risk, so monthly self-exams, a yearly professional exam, and sun protection are important.
Incorrect. Watching for changing moles is good teaching, but it does not answer whether the father's diagnosis changes the client's risk.
Incorrect. Risk is higher, but genetic testing is not routine for most families; regular skin checks and sun protection are the standard response.
questions.rationale: Genetics and family history are risk factors that cannot be changed, and a parent with melanoma raises a client's own risk. Knowing this identifies the client as someone who needs extra teaching: monthly self-exams, a yearly professional skin exam, and strict sun protection. Focusing only on sunscreen is tempting because UV is the main cause of skin cancer, but risk factors combine. The nurse uses the news as a teaching moment.
questions.takeaway: A parent with melanoma raises the client's risk: teach self-exams, yearly professional exams, and sun protection.

questions.hintStrategy: The best answer meets every requirement; one missing element makes an option wrong.
questions.stem: The parent of a 7-year-old who will attend an outdoor swim camp asks the nurse which sunscreen to buy and how to use it. Which recommendation is best?
options: Broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30, applied once each morning before camp
Broad-spectrum SPF 50, reapplied every 2 hours, with no need for water resistance
Broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30, reapplied only after the child swims
Broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30, reapplied every 2 hours and after swimming
optionRationales: Incorrect. The product is correct, but water-resistant does not mean all day; one morning application wears off during swimming and sweating.
Incorrect. Broad-spectrum and reapplication are right, but a child at swim camp needs a water-resistant product that stays on in the water.
Incorrect. Reapplying after swimming is right, but sunscreen also needs reapplication about every 2 hours even when the child stays dry.
Correct. Broad-spectrum (UVA and UVB), water-resistant SPF 30 or higher, reapplied about every 2 hours and after swimming, is the recommendation.
questions.rationale: Effective sunscreen is broad-spectrum (blocking UVA and UVB), SPF 30 or higher, and water-resistant for swimming or sweating. Water-resistant does not mean all day: it must be reapplied about every 2 hours and after swimming, sweating, or towel drying. A higher SPF is tempting, but without water resistance it washes off at a swim camp. A swim shirt helps, but all exposed skin still needs sunscreen.
questions.takeaway: Swimming: broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30+, reapplied about every 2 hours and after swimming or toweling.

questions.hintContent: Consider whether cold weather or clouds change UV exposure.
questions.hintStrategy: In "indicates understanding" SATA, eliminate statements containing common sun myths.
questions.stem: A family is planning a week-long ski trip. After the nurse teaches about sun protection, which statements by the parents indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “We won't need sunscreen because it's winter and the air is cold.”
“We'll use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher on any skin that is exposed.”
“We'll reapply sunscreen about every 2 hours, and after the kids get sweaty.”
“We'll put on sunscreen even on cloudy days because UV passes through clouds.”
“Our son has darker skin than the rest of us, so he can skip sunscreen.”
“We'll pack UV-blocking sunglasses for everyone in the family.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cold air does not block UV, so sunscreen is still needed in winter.
Correct. Broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher is recommended for exposed skin.
Correct. Sunscreen should be reapplied about every 2 hours and after sweating.
Correct. UV passes through clouds, so sunscreen is needed on cloudy days.
Incorrect. All skin tones need sun protection.
Correct. UV-blocking sunglasses are part of sun protection.
questions.rationale: Sun protection is needed whenever there is UV exposure, regardless of temperature, cloud cover, or skin tone. The family should use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin, reapply about every 2 hours and after sweating, use UV-blocking sunglasses and hats, and seek shade when possible. Linking sun risk to heat is the tempting error, because people feel the sun's warmth rather than its UV. Exempting a child with darker skin is also wrong, since every skin tone is at risk.
questions.takeaway: UV does not depend on temperature or clouds, and every skin tone needs protection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client who plans to spend most of the summer gardening is being discharged with the medications shown in the exhibit. For which medications should the nurse include teaching about possible skin thinning or increased sun sensitivity? Select all that apply.
options: Docusate sodium
Griseofulvin
Doxycycline
Prednisone
Acetaminophen
optionRationales: Incorrect. Docusate, a stool softener, is not linked to skin thinning or photosensitivity.
Correct. Antifungals such as griseofulvin can cause photosensitivity, so the client may burn much faster.
Correct. Antibiotics such as doxycycline can cause photosensitivity, so the client may burn much faster.
Correct. Corticosteroids such as prednisone may thin the skin and increase sun sensitivity.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen is not one of the medication groups linked to skin thinning or photosensitivity.
questions.rationale: Steroids, antibiotics, chemotherapy, and antifungals may thin the skin or cause photosensitivity, meaning the skin burns much faster in the sun. A client taking prednisone, doxycycline, and griseofulvin who plans to garden all summer needs teaching on long sleeves, a wide-brimmed hat, shade, and broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher reapplied often. The nurse does not tell the client to stop the medicines. Acetaminophen may seem to belong because it is taken regularly, but it is not in these drug groups.
questions.takeaway: Steroids, antibiotics, chemotherapy, and antifungals can thin skin or cause photosensitivity; pair them with sun-protection teaching.

questions.hintContent: Recall how skin conditions and skin cancer present differently in darker skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any statement that uses "always" or claims a skin tone needs no protection.
questions.stem: The nurse is presenting skin health information at a community center whose members mostly have darker skin tones. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Sun exposure can make dark facial patches called melasma even darker
Check the palms, soles, and nails, where melanoma is more often found in darker skin
Skin cancer can occur in every skin tone and is often found later in darker skin
Eczema and psoriasis always look bright red, whatever the skin tone
Darker skin has enough melanin that sunscreen is not needed
Thick scars called keloids can grow beyond the edges of the original wound
optionRationales: Correct. Melasma is more common in darker skin and darkens with sun exposure.
Correct. In darker skin, melanoma is more often found in low-sun areas such as the palms, soles, and nails.
Correct. All clients are at risk regardless of skin tone, and skin cancer in darker skin is often diagnosed later.
Incorrect. In darker skin, these conditions may look purple, gray, or dark brown rather than red.
Incorrect. Sun protection is needed for every skin tone.
Correct. Darker skin is more prone to keloids, which grow past the wound edge.
questions.rationale: Darker skin has more melanin, but it is not immune to skin cancer, and cancer is often found later, partly because melanoma tends to appear in low-sun areas such as the palms, soles, and nails. Darker skin is also more prone to keloids, pseudofolliculitis, dermatosis papulosa nigra, and melasma, which worsens with sun. The sunscreen statement is tempting because more melanin does give some protection, but every skin tone needs sun protection. Inflammatory conditions may look purple, gray, or dark brown rather than red.
questions.takeaway: Darker skin: cancer still occurs (check palms, soles, nails), keloids and melasma are more common, and redness may look purple or gray.

questions.hintContent: Recall which areas are easy to miss and which changes matter most.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any instruction with "only" that narrows the exam.
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 40-year-old client how to perform a monthly skin self-examination. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Examine only the areas that are usually exposed to the sun
Check only the moles that are larger than a pencil eraser
Check the scalp, ears, and back of the neck, with a partner's help if needed
Use good lighting with a full-length mirror and a hand mirror
Look at the soles of the feet, between the toes, and the nails
Note any sore that has not healed and any new or changing spot
optionRationales: Incorrect. The trunk, chest, and feet must also be checked, not just sun-exposed areas.
Incorrect. Any changing mole needs evaluation, regardless of size.
Correct. The scalp, ears, and neck are sun-exposed and easy to miss; a partner can help.
Correct. Good light and mirrors let the client see hard-to-view areas.
Correct. The feet, toes, and nails must be included, especially in darker skin.
Correct. Non-healing sores and new or changing spots are warning signs.
questions.rationale: Monthly self-exams help clients learn what their normal skin looks like so they notice changes early. Teach the client to use good light, mirrors, or a partner, to check sun-exposed areas, and also to check the trunk, chest, and feet, including the soles, between the toes, and the nails. The client should look for new spots, sores that do not heal, and moles that fit the ABCDE rule. Limiting the exam to large moles is tempting because of the 6-mm rule, but evolving moles of any size matter.
questions.takeaway: Monthly self-exam: good light and mirrors, head to toe including soles, toes, and nails; look for new, changing, or non-healing spots.

questions.hintContent: Consider whether removing one cancer changes the skin's overall risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each instruction for accuracy about this specific cancer type.
questions.stem: A 63-year-old client had a basal cell carcinoma removed from the forearm last week, and the margins were clear. Which instructions should the nurse include in the follow-up teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Stop sunscreen on the treated arm because the cancer has been removed
Do monthly skin self-exams and report any new, changing, or non-healing spots
Continue to use broad-spectrum sunscreen on the treated arm and all exposed skin
Expect the cancer to spread to the organs, so plan for scans every month
Keep regular professional skin exams as scheduled by the provider
Wear a wide-brimmed hat and long sleeves when working outdoors
optionRationales: Incorrect. Removing one cancer does not protect the skin from new UV damage.
Correct. A client who has had one skin cancer should monitor for new lesions.
Correct. Sun protection continues after treatment because UV damage that causes skin cancer is cumulative.
Incorrect. Basal cell carcinoma rarely spreads, so monthly scans are not expected.
Correct. Professional skin exams continue after a skin cancer diagnosis.
Correct. Hats and protective clothing are key parts of sun protection.
questions.rationale: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, grows slowly, and rarely spreads, so clear margins are reassuring. However, the sun damage that caused it affects the client's skin everywhere, so ongoing sun protection, monthly self-exams, and regular professional exams are needed. Stopping sunscreen on the treated arm is tempting because the cancer is "gone," but the risk of new cancers remains. Expecting spread confuses basal cell carcinoma with melanoma.
questions.takeaway: After a skin cancer is removed, keep up sun protection, monthly self-exams, and professional skin exams.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the health history of a client at a skin cancer screening. Refer to the exhibit. Which of this client's risk factors for skin cancer and skin damage can the client change? Select all that apply.
options: Fair skin and light eyes
Age of 64 years
Smoking 1 pack per day
Mother's history of melanoma
Golfing without sunscreen
Weekly tanning-bed use
optionRationales: Incorrect. Skin and eye color are inherited and cannot be changed.
Incorrect. Age cannot be changed.
Correct. Smoking contributes to extrinsic skin damage, including precancerous changes, and can be stopped.
Incorrect. Family history is a fixed genetic risk factor.
Correct. The client can use sunscreen, a hat, protective clothing, and shade while golfing.
Correct. Tanning-bed use is a modifiable source of UV exposure.
questions.rationale: Some risk factors cannot be changed (genetics, family history, skin tone, age), and they identify clients who need extra teaching and screening. Other risk factors can be changed: UV exposure from the sun or tanning beds, and smoking, which contributes to extrinsic aging and precancerous changes. Teaching focuses on the modifiable factors while increasing screening for the fixed ones. Fair skin is tempting because it is a strong risk factor, but it cannot be changed, only protected.
questions.takeaway: Modifiable skin risks: UV exposure (sun, tanning beds) and smoking; genetics, skin tone, and age are fixed.

questions.hintContent: Identify which statements repeat common sun-protection myths.
questions.hintStrategy: In "indicates understanding" SATA, any statement promising long-lasting or "base" protection is a red flag.
questions.stem: After a skin cancer prevention class, several high school students share what they learned. Which statements indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “Tanning beds are not a safe way to get some color.”
“A base tan before vacation will protect me from burning.”
“I should look for shade from about 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.”
“A tan means my skin has already been damaged.”
“Water-resistant sunscreen lasts all day at the pool.”
optionRationales: Correct. Tanning beds give off damaging UV radiation.
Incorrect. A base tan is not protection.
Correct. Seeking shade roughly from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. reduces UV exposure.
Correct. A tan is the skin's response to DNA damage that has already happened.
Incorrect. Water-resistant sunscreen still needs reapplying about every 2 hours and after swimming or toweling.
questions.rationale: Most skin cancers are preventable, and habits formed in adolescence matter because UV damage builds up for life. Students should know that a tan signals damage, tanning beds are never safe, and shade is important from about 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Water-resistant sunscreen is the tempting wrong statement because the label sounds long-lasting, but it still wears off and needs reapplying. A base tan does not prevent burns or cancer.
questions.takeaway: No tan is a safe tan; seek shade 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and reapply even water-resistant sunscreen.
